Neural-network quantum states for many-body physics

Matija Medvidović Email: matija.medvidovic@columbia.edu Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, 162 5th Avenue, New York, NY 10010, USA Affiliation: Department of Physics, Columbia University, NY 10027, USA    Javier Robledo Moreno Email: j.robledomoreno@ibm.com Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, 162 5th Avenue, New York, NY 10010, USA Affiliation: Center for Quantum Phenomena, Department of Physics, New York University, 726 Broadway, New York, NY 10003, USA Affiliation: IBM Quantum, IBM Research - 1101 Kitchawan Rd, Yorktown Heights, NY 10598, USA
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Variational quantum calculations have borrowed many tools and algorithms from the machine learning community in the recent years. Leveraging great expressive power and efficient gradient-based optimization, researchers have shown that trial states inspired by deep learning problems can accurately model many-body correlated phenomena in spin, fermionic and qubit systems. In this review, we derive the central equations of different flavors variational Monte Carlo (VMC) approaches, including ground state search, time evolution and overlap optimization, and discuss data-driven tasks like quantum state tomography. An emphasis is put on the geometry of the variational manifold as well as bottlenecks in practical implementations. An overview of recent results of first-principles ground-state and real-time calculations is provided.

I Introduction

The remarkable progress in machine learning has inevitably trickled down and revolutionized the physical sciences [1]. In particular, machine learning has shown great promise for the numerical study of quantum many-body systems [2]. Machine learning and the quantum many-body problem share many similarities. Both fields are established in the intersection between applied linear algebra in large vector spaces, probability and statistics, and challenging optimization tasks. Therefore, it is only natural to wonder whether machine learning techniques can be applied to tackle the quantum many-body problem and further our knowledge of the underlying physical processes that govern the collective behaviour of interacting quantum particles. This review specifically addresses the application of machine learning techniques to existing numerical many-body methods to improve their accuracy and efficiency.

The approximation of many-body wave functions by neural networks is one of the most promising avenues in the field [3]. This parametric family is referred to as neural quantum states (NQS). Neural networks provide a compact and accurate representation of the exponentially-scaling components of the many-body state. The accurate representation of quantum states is only possible thanks to the large expressive power of neural neural networks to represent complex functions [4, 5, 6]. It has been empirically and theoretically demonstrated that neural networks can approximate relevant quantum states whose entanglement entropy scales with the number of degrees of freedom of the problem [7, 8, 9, 10, 11] (volume-law scaling), while traditional variational states like the matrix product state [12] (MPS) are not capable of efficiently describing highly-entangled states [13]. More generally, it has been shown that any efficiently-contractable tensor network (TN) state can be efficiently mapped into a neural network [9, 10].

The approximation of quantum states by neural networks relies on the gradient-based optimization of the weights and biases, since expectation values, overlaps and gradients thereof requires the use of Monte Carlo stochastic techniques for their estimation. It is this optimization where the greatest challenges for NQS arise, compared to other many-body methods like the density matrix renormalization group [12] (DMRG) to optimize the parameters of a MPS. The characterization of the parameter optimization and its improvements remains an active field of research [14, 15, 16, 17, 18].

Despite these challenges, NQS have demonstrated an enormous potential in the description of challenging many-body problems, including systems of interacting spins [19, 20, 21, 22, 20, 23] and systems of interacting fermions [24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29]. These techniques have also demonstrated outstanding levels of accuracy in the description of the time evolution of many-body systems [30, 31, 32, 14, 33], the simulation of quantum circuits [34] and quantum state tomography tasks [35].

Other excellent review papers in the field are available, focusing on the practical implementation of these techniques [36], electronic structure problems [37] and neural-network architectures and applications [38].

This review introduces, in a self-contained and pedagogical manner, the main concepts and theory behind the description of many-body wave functions using neural network approximations, their optimization and applications. The goal of this review is to provide the reader with the basis to understand the literature in the topic. Section II introduces the general framework of variational Monte Carlo (Sec. II.1) and the need for Monte Carlo techniques to estimate expectation values of observables (Sec. II.2) and gradients with respect to variational parameters. Section II also introduces the main sampling methods required to estimate such expectation values (Sec. II.3) and four scenarios for variational parameter optimization: ground state search (Sec. II.4), time evolution (Sec. II.5), overlap optimization (Sec. II.6) and maximum likelihood estimation (Sec. II.7). These four techniques are the basis for the applications described in later sections. Section II ends with a description of the fundamental concepts behind the imposition of symmetries in NQS calculations (Sec. II.8). Section III focuses on the application of the concepts introduced in Section II to relevant many-body systems, including the study of the ground state properties of systems of interacting spins (Sec. III.1), and systems of interacting fermions (Sec. III.2), as well as the unitary transformation of many-body wave functions to describe the time evolution of man-body systems and to simulate quantum circuits (Sec. III.3). Sec. III concludes with a description of the application of NQS to the problem of quantum state tomography (Sec. III.4). The scope of this manuscript is summarized in Fig. 1.

II Neural networks and Monte Carlo

In this section, we introduce the variational Monte Carlo (VMC) algorithm, motivating the optimization problem through the basic variational theorem of quantum mechanics (see Fig. 1). Stochastic estimators of Hilbert-space operators are introduced as a necessary approximation of full expectation values and Monte Carlo sampling algorithms are motivated as an essential tool in that process. We discuss both imaginary and real-time calculations through a common geometrical picture of Hilbert-space trajectories projected onto a variational manifold. Gradient-based optimization techniques of increasing complexity are introduced as a consequence of discretizing these trajectories. Finally, some common convergence metrics are proposed and discussed.

II.1 Variational quantum state definition

In order to follow through with the program laid out by the variational theorem, we consider a general Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}, spanned by basis {|𝐱⟩}\{\ket{\xx}\} of product states, or their completely symmetrized (or antisymmetrized) versions for systems of indistinguishable bosons (or fermions). The set of basis states satisfies the closure relation 𝟙=∑𝐱|𝐱⟩⟨𝐱|\mathbbm{1}=\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}}\outerproduct{\xx}{\xx}. The following discussion applies to a wide variety of many-body systems. Some examples of systems and bases that they use to span the many-body Hilbert space include:

  • •

    Spin systems: |𝐱⟩↦|↑↑…↑⟩,|↓↑…↑⟩​…\ket{\xx}\mapsto\ket{\uparrow\uparrow\hdots\uparrow},\ket{\downarrow\uparrow\hdots\uparrow}\ldots

    The basis is composed by all possible tensor products of single spin states in the reference quantization axis.

  • •

    Qubit systems: |𝐱⟩↦|00​…​0⟩,|10​…​0⟩​…\ket{\xx}\mapsto\ket{0 0 \hdots 0},\ket{1 0 \hdots 0}\ldots

    The basis is composed by all possible tensor products of single qubit states in the computational basis.

  • •

    Fermionic systems: |𝐱⟩↦∏p=1M(ap†)np​|∅⟩.\ket{\xx}\mapsto\prod_{p=1}^{M}\left(a^{\dagger}_{p}\right)^{n_{p}}\ket{\varnothing}\,.

    The ket |∅⟩\ket{\varnothing} refers to the Fock vacuum and ap†a^{\dagger}_{p} is the creation operator that adds a fermion to fermionic mode (or single-particle state or spin orbital) pp. MM labels the number of single-particle states that span the Hilbert space. n∈{0,1}Mn\in\{0,1\}^{M} labels the occupancies of each fermionic mode. Many-body Hilbert space basis is obtained by the populating available fermionic modes in all possible ways. For a review of second quantization see Ref. [39].

  • •

    Bosonic systems: |𝐱⟩↦∏p=1M(bp†)np​|∅⟩.\ket{\xx}\mapsto\prod_{p=1}^{M}\left(b^{\dagger}_{p}\right)^{n_{p}}\ket{\varnothing}\,.

    The ket |∅⟩\ket{\varnothing} refers to the Fock vacuum and bp†b^{\dagger}_{p} is the creation operator that adds a boson to bosonic mode (or single-particle state) pp. MM labels the number of single-particle states that span the Hilbert space and NN the number of bosons in the system. n∈{0,N}Mn\in\{0,N\}^{M} such that ∑p=1Mnp=N\sum_{p=1}^{M}n_{p}=N labels the occupancies of each bosonic mode. Many-body Hilbert space basis is obtained by the populating available bosonic modes in all possible ways. For a review of second quantization see Ref. [39].

Since the dimension of the Hilbert space for the above many-body systems grows exponentially or combinatorially with system size, a trial wave function based on the direct enumeration of all of the wave function amplitudes is not feasible beyond small system sizes. Instead, we introduce a general unnormalized variational quantum state

|ψθ⟩=∑𝐱ψθ​(𝐱)​|𝐱⟩,\ket{\psi_\theta}=\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}}\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})\ket{\xx}\;, (1)

defined on the basis 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} and parameterized by PP real or complex parameters θ\theta. Without loss of generality, we assume θ∈ℝP\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{P}. For a discussion of all the possible cases, we refer the interested reader to an excellent overview in Ref. [40]. The set ℳψ={|ψθ⟩|θ∈ℝP}\mathcal{M}_{\psi}=\left\{\ket{\psi_\theta}|\;\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{P}\right\} is called the variational manifold and, by definition, contains all states exactly representable by the trial state ψθ\psi_{\theta}. The goal of the techniques presented in following sections is to find the set of variational parameters θ\theta such that |ψθ⟩|\psi_{\theta}\rangle approximates a target many-body state as closely as possible. The variational state |ψθ⟩\ket{\psi_\theta} is defined by its amplitudes, which are functions of the basis element labels 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}

ψθ:𝐱→ℂ.\psi_{\theta}:{\mathbf{x}}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}. (2)

We require that the function ψθ\psi_{\theta} can be evaluated at a polynomial cost in the number of degrees of freedom of the problem (number of spins, qubits, single-particle basis elements, particle number etc.). This requirement is the root of the approximate nature of the approach. The most general variational state ψθ\psi_{\theta} is that represented by the lookup table of wave-function amplitudes for each basis state. However, due to the exponential or combinatorial growth of the Hilbert space dimension, this lookup table requires the storage of exponentially or combinatorially many amplitudes, making it not efficiently computable.

A neural quantum state is a variational wave function for which ψθ\psi_{\theta} is partially or completely defined by a neural network whose weights and biases are part of the variational parameters θ\theta. A neural network defines a parametrized model family, whose functional form relies on the sequential composition of layers of parametrized transformations [41]. They also satisfy a universal approximation theorem [4, 5, 6], that states that for a sufficiently-large number of parameters, a neural network can approximate any target function to any specified accuracy.

II.2 Estimation of expectation values: the local observable trick

The characterization of the physical properties of the many-body system (like the energy, susceptibilities…), as well as the parameter search for ψθ\psi_{\theta} requires the efficient computation of expectation values of the form:

⟨Q⟩ψθ=⟨ψθ|​Q​|ψθ⟩⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩.\expectationvalue{Q}_{\psi_{\theta}}=\frac{\bra{\psi_\theta}Q\ket{\psi_\theta}}{\innerproduct{\psi_\theta}{\psi_\theta}}\;. (3)

where QQ is a generic many-body operator. The direct calculation of the numerator and denominator of the expectation value require the evaluation of a sum that contains a number of elements that grows exponentially/combinatorially with the number of degrees of freedom of the problem. Evaluating Hilbert space averages in Eq. 3 cannot be performed exactly. However, estimates can be made through Monte Carlo summation/integration. In general, expressions of the following form can be estimated

⟨f⁡(𝐱)⟩𝐱∼p=∑𝐱p⁡(𝐱)​f​(𝐱)∑𝐱p⁡(𝐱)≈1Ns​∑i=1Nsf⁡(𝐱i)\expectationvalue{f(\xx)}_{{\mathbf{x}}\sim p}=\frac{\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}}p({\mathbf{x}})f({\mathbf{x}})}{\sum_{\mathbf{x}}p({\mathbf{x}})}\approx\frac{1}{N_{\text{s}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{s}}}f({\mathbf{x}}_{i}) (4)

using NsN_{\text{s}} samples from the (unnormalized) distribution p⁡(𝐱)p({\mathbf{x}}). This is a direct consequence of the Central Limit Theorem [42]. To make contact with the quantum VMC setting, we rewrite the energy expectation in Eq. 3 as:

⟨Q⟩ψθ=∑𝐱⟨ψθ|𝐱⟩​⟨𝐱|​Q​|ψθ⟩∑𝐱′⟨ψθ|𝐱′⟩​⟨𝐱′|ψθ⟩=∑𝐱pθ​(𝐱)​QL​(𝐱)\expectationvalue{Q}_{\psi_{\theta}}=\frac{\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\innerproduct{\psi_\theta}{\xx}\bra{\xx}Q\ket{\psi_\theta}}{\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}}\innerproduct{\psi_\theta}{\xx'}\innerproduct{\xx'}{\psi_\theta}}=\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\;p_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})\,Q_{L}({\mathbf{x}}) (5)

where

pθ​(𝐱)∝|ψθ​(𝐱)|2andQL​(𝐱)=⟨𝐱|​Q​|ψθ⟩⟨𝐱|ψθ⟩p_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})\propto\left|\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})\right|^{2}\quad\text{and}\quad Q_{L}({\mathbf{x}})=\frac{\bra{\xx}Q\ket{\psi_\theta}}{\innerproduct{\xx}{\psi_\theta}} (6)

defines the local observable function QL​(𝐱)Q_{L}({\mathbf{x}}). Note that the evaluation of the local observable requires the calculation of the overlap ⟨𝐱|​Q​|ψθ⟩\bra{\xx}Q\ket{\psi_\theta}. This is only possible if for every basis state |𝐱′⟩\ket{\xx'} the number of connected non-zero matrix elements to |𝐱⟩\ket{\xx} grows at most polynomially with the number of degrees of freedom of the problem. The unbiased estimator to the expectation value of QQ is then obtained as the empirical average (Eq. 4) of the associated local observable QLQ_{L} evaluated at basis state configurations 𝐱i{\mathbf{x}}_{i} sampled from the state:

⟨Q⟩ψθ≈1Ns​∑i=1NsQL​(𝐱i)=⟨QL​(𝐱)⟩𝐱∼|ψθ|2.\expectationvalue{Q}_{\psi_{\theta}}\approx\frac{1}{N_{\text{s}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{s}}}Q_{L}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})=\expectationvalue{Q_L(\xx)}_{{\mathbf{x}}\sim|\psi_{\theta}|^{2}}\;. (7)

An operator of special relevance is the Hamiltonian of the system HH. The associated local observable received the name of local energy EL=⟨𝐱|H|ψθ⟩∕⟨𝐱|ψθ⟩E_{L}=\ifrac{\matrixelement{\xx}{H}{\psi_\theta}}{\innerproduct{\xx}{\psi_\theta}}. An overview of relevant sampling-related algorithms and details is given in Sec. II.3. In all cases, efficient calculation of many decorrelated samples is crucial for correctly resolving gradients and other averages.

II.3 Sampling

As noted in Sec. II.4, Monte Carlo sampling is used for evaluation of relevant averages in Eq. 16. The goal is to obtain samples {𝐱i:i=1,…,Ns}∼p(𝐱)\left\{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}:i=1,\ldots,N_{\text{s}}\right\}\sim p({\mathbf{x}}) to evaluate sums of the type given in Eq. 4, given an analytical probability distribution p⁡(𝐱)p({\mathbf{x}}). Most commonly, well-established Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) black-box samplers from classical statistics literature are used [43]. However, with certain restricted classes of trial states called autoregressive states, efficient and exact sampling is possible. We review both cases in the following section.

II.3.1 Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling

Often, MCMC algorithms are run in two steps – first a new sample 𝐱′{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime} is proposed from a current one 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} and then it is either accepted or rejected according to the Metropolis-Hastings [44, 45] probability:

paccept=min⁡(1,p∕(∕𝐱∕′∕)∕p∕(∕𝐱∕))p_{\text{accept}}=\min\left(1,\ifrac{p({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})}{p({\mathbf{x}})}\right)\, (8)

assuming the usual constraints of detailed balance and ergodicity. It can be shown that biasing the random walk of proposed states with Eq. 8 is guaranteed to converge to the correct distribution p⁡(𝐱)p({\mathbf{x}}). We refer the the detail-oriented reader to Refs. [46, 47]. In the context of wavefunction-baseed variational calculations such as VMC, the probability distribution is given by p⁡(𝐱)∝|ψθ​(𝐱)|2p({\mathbf{x}})\propto\left|\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})\right|^{2}. Note that in the Metropolis-Hastings sampling procedure the probability distribution pp is not required to be normalized. Consequently, when using a Metropolis-Hastings sampler, the trial state does not need to be explicitly normalized.

In the context of VMC, the most popular choice of MCMC scheme is the simple local Metropolis sampler, relying on small local changes to states 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} to propose new ones 𝐱′{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}. Depending on the physical system at hand, the simplest and most common update schemes can take different forms.

For systems with discrete degrees of freedom such as spins, we can simply flip a random spin in the state 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} to obtain 𝐱′{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}. This is the single-spin flip update. If particle number or magnetization conservation needs to be enforced, pairs of up-down spins can be flipped simultaneously. We note that a sequence of such updates can be concatenated into a single larger update if acceptance rates are high enough.

For some systems, an efficient cluster update scheme can be constructed, greatly improving state space exploration. This is especially useful in the case of systems near criticality, where the correlation length is large and single-spin updates are inefficient. A popular cluster update scheme is the Wolff algorithm [48] for the Ising model. For a review of cluster algorithms, we refer the reader to Ref. [46, 47].

In the case of continuous degrees of freedom such as electron positions 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} in a molecular system, a small local update is usually defined as

𝐱′=𝐱+δ​𝐱,whereδ​𝐱∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ2).{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}={\mathbf{x}}+\delta{\mathbf{x}}\;,\quad\text{where}\quad\delta{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma^{2})\;. (9)

The normal distribution variance is set by Σ2\Sigma^{2}, a hyperparameter tuned to achieve a certain acceptance rate. If the variance is too small, acceptance rates are high but individual updates stay too close to the original state, halting efficient exploration of the state space. If it is too large, acceptance rate drops because 𝐱′{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime} can randomly hop too far outside of high probability regions and the sampler becomes inefficient. This version of the local Metropolis scheme is sometimes called the random walk Metropolis (RWM) algorithm.

Another option for continuous systems is Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) [49, 50, 51], offering a systematic way of making large steps in proposals while still keeping acceptance probabilities high, unlike RWM. This can result in lower MCMC autocorrelation times, allowing for treatments of larger systems with less overall runtime spent on sampling. For a probability distribution p⁡(𝐱)p({\mathbf{x}}), HMC augments the configuration space with artificial momentum variables 𝝅=(π1,…,πN)∼𝒩⁡(0,M)\bm{\pi}=(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{N})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,M):

p⁡(𝐱)∝∫dN𝝅​exp⁡{−12​𝝅⊤​M−1​𝝅+ln⁡p⁡(𝐱)}p({\mathbf{x}})\propto\int\differential[N]{\bm{\pi}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\bm{\pi}^{\top}M^{-1}\bm{\pi}+\ln p({\mathbf{x}})\right\} (10)

for some positive-definite matrix MM. The integrand in Eq. 10 can be read as an effective Boltzmann distribution e−β​H~e^{-\beta\widetilde{H}} induced by an effective classical Hamiltonian β​H~​(𝐱,𝝅)\beta\widetilde{H}({\mathbf{x}},\bm{\pi}). MCMC proposals can then be constructed through numerical integration of Hamilton’s equations, starting from the current state 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} – particles in equilibrium following classical equations of motion conserve the desired Boltzmann distribution. Readers interested in an intuitive geometrical picture are referred to an excellent review in Ref. [52].

II.3.2 Autoregressive sampling

Autoregressive sampling is an exact and embarrassingly parallel algorithm for sampling probability distributions p⁡(𝐱)p({\mathbf{x}}) of the special form

p⁡(𝐱)=p⁡(𝐱1,…,𝐱N)=∏ip⁡(𝐱i|𝐱<i)==p(𝐱1)p(𝐱2|𝐱1)⋯p(𝐱N|𝐱N−1,…,𝐱2,𝐱1),\begin{gathered}p({\mathbf{x}})=p({\mathbf{x}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{N})=\prod_{i}p({\mathbf{x}}_{i}|{\mathbf{x}}_{<i})=\\ =p({\mathbf{x}}_{1})\,p({\mathbf{x}}_{2}|{\mathbf{x}}_{1})\,\cdots\,p({\mathbf{x}}_{N}|{\mathbf{x}}_{N-1},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{2},{\mathbf{x}}_{1})\;,\end{gathered} (11)

where we have defined the set 𝐱<i={𝐱1,…,𝐱i−1}{\mathbf{x}}_{<i}=\left\{{\mathbf{x}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{i-1}\right\} by slight abuse of notation. If a distribution can be written in the form of Eq. 11, then a simple ancestral sampling approach can be used by iterating the following two steps for each i=1,…,N−1i=1,\ldots,N-1:

  1. 1.

    Sample 𝐱i∼p⁡(𝐱i|𝐱<i){\mathbf{x}}_{i}\sim p({\mathbf{x}}_{i}|{\mathbf{x}}_{<i}) and concatenate to 𝐱<i{\mathbf{x}}_{<i}.

  2. 2.

    Use samples to define p⁡(𝐱i+1|𝐱<i+1)p({\mathbf{x}}_{i+1}|{\mathbf{x}}_{<i+1}).

We note that this procedure relies on being able to efficiently and exactly sample each conditional p⁡(𝐱i|𝐱<i)p({\mathbf{x}}_{i}|{\mathbf{x}}_{<i}). As a consequence, components 𝐱i{\mathbf{x}}_{i} have to be chosen to be sufficiently low-dimensional.

Some additional choices have to be made when generalizing autoregressive distributions to complex wavefunctions ψ⁡(𝐱)\psi({\mathbf{x}}). For example, authors in Ref. [53] choose to add a phase function globally by multiplying the expression in Eq. 11 by ei​ϕ​(𝐱)e^{i\phi({\mathbf{x}})} where ϕ\phi is unrestricted while authors in Refs. [54, 55], choose to further decompose ϕ⁡(𝐱)=∑iϕ⁡(𝐱i|𝐱<i)\phi({\mathbf{x}})=\sum_{i}\phi({\mathbf{x}}_{i}|{\mathbf{x}}_{<i}). Either way, the only restriction to including the phase is that |ψ⁡(𝐱)|2|\psi({\mathbf{x}})|^{2} has to have the structure of Eq. 11.

II.4 Stochastic optimization

The goal in variational calculations is to minimize the energy expectation

E=E⁡(θ)=⟨ψθ|H|ψθ⟩⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩≥E0.E=E(\theta)=\frac{\expectationvalue{H}{\psi_\theta}}{\innerproduct{\psi_\theta}{\psi_\theta}}\geq E_{0}\;. (12)

The energy in Eq. 12 is now a function of parameters θ\theta and an upper bound to the true ground state energy E0E_{0} for all θ\theta. Our task then boils down to finding optimal parameters θopt=argminE​(θ)\theta_{\text{opt}}=\argmin E(\theta) that best approximate the ground state within ℳψ\mathcal{M}_{\psi}. Modern gradient-based optimization methods are often used to find θopt\theta_{\text{opt}} in an iterative manner, starting from an initial guess. The expression for the relevant gradients g=∇θE​(θ)g=\nabla_{\theta}E(\theta) can be obtained by direct computation starting from Eq. 12. However, in this review, we choose to derive a more general geometrical approach to this optimization problem from a physical point of view – imaginary time evolution. The remainder of this section is devoted to connecting these ideas from statistical physics to such optimizers.

Imaginary time evolution well-known trick for systematically filtering out ground state |0⟩\ket{0} components out of arbitrary trial states |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}, provided that the trial state is not orthogonal to the ground state:

|0⟩∝limτ→∞e−τ​H​|ψ⟩,\ket{0}\propto\lim_{\tau\rightarrow\infty}e^{-\tau H}\ket{\psi}\,, (13)

which can be made obvious by formally expanding |ψ⟩=∑ncn​|n⟩\ket{\psi}=\sum_{n}c_{n}\ket{n} in the energy eigenbasis H​|n⟩=En​|n⟩H\ket{n}=E_{n}\ket{n}. We then have

e−τ​H​|ψ⟩=∑ncn​e−τ​En​|n⟩∝∝|0⟩+∑n>0cnc0​e−τ⁡(En−E0)​|n⟩,\begin{gathered}e^{-\tau H}\ket{\psi}=\sum_{n}c_{n}\;e^{-\tau E_{n}}\ket{n}\propto\\ \propto\ket{0}+\sum_{n>0}\;\frac{c_{n}}{c_{0}}\;e^{-\tau(E_{n}-E_{0})}\ket{n}\;,\end{gathered} (14)

assuming a non-degenerate ground state and c0=⟨0|ψ⟩≠0c_{0}=\innerproduct{0}{\psi}\neq 0. The second term in Eq. 14 vanishes under the τ→∞\tau\rightarrow\infty limit because En>E0E_{n}>E_{0} for all n>0n>0 by definition.

We apply imaginary time evolution to our trial state in small increments: e−τ​H=e−δ​τ​H⋯e−δ​τ​He^{-\tau H}=e^{-\delta\tau H}\cdots e^{-\delta\tau H}. In other words, we iteratively update our parameters θ′=θ+δ​θ\theta^{\prime}=\theta+\delta\theta so that:

|ψθ+δ​θ⟩∝e−δ​τ​H​|ψθ⟩,\ket{\psi_{\theta+ \delta\theta}}\propto e^{-\delta\tau H}\ket{\psi_\theta}\;, (15)

where the proportionality sign accounts for the possible change in the overall normalization.

Expanding both sides in Eq. 15 to first order in small parameter increments, we obtain S​θ˙=−gS\,\dot{\theta}=-g in the limit of δ​τ→0\delta\tau\rightarrow 0, where θ˙=dθ/dτ\dot{\theta}=\nicefrac{{\differential\theta}}{{\differential\tau}} and

Sμ​ν=2​Re⁡{⟨𝒪μ†​𝒪ν⟩−⟨𝒪μ†⟩​⟨𝒪ν⟩},gμ=2​Re⁡{⟨𝒪μ†​H⟩−⟨𝒪μ†⟩​⟨H⟩}.\begin{gathered}S_{\mu\nu}=2\Re{ \ev{\OO^\dagger_\mu\OO_\nu} - \ev{\OO^\dagger_\mu} \ev{\OO_\nu\vphantom{\OO^\dagger_\mu} } }\;,\\ g_{\mu}=2\Re{ \ev{\OO^\dagger_\mu H} - \ev{\OO^\dagger_\mu} \ev{H \vphantom{\OO^\dagger_\mu} } }\;.\end{gathered} (16)

In Eq. 16, μ,ν,…\mu,\nu,\ldots indices denote parameter dependence. Averages ⟨⋅⟩≡⟨ψθ|⋅|ψθ⟩/⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩\expectationvalue{\cdot}\equiv\nicefrac{{\bra{\psi_\theta}\cdot\ket{\psi_\theta}}}{{\innerproduct{\psi_\theta}{\psi_\theta}}} are performed with respect to the trial state itself at imaginary time τ\tau. Diagonal operators 𝒪μ\mathcal{O}_{\mu} are defined by ∂θμ|ψθ⟩=𝒪μ​|ψθ⟩\partial_{\theta^{\mu}}\ket{\psi_\theta}=\mathcal{O}_{\mu}\ket{\psi_\theta} or

𝒪μ=∑𝐱∂ln⁡ψθ∂θμ​(𝐱)​|𝐱⟩⟨𝐱|.\mathcal{O}_{\mu}=\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}}\frac{\partial\ln\psi_{\theta}}{\partial\theta^{\mu}}({\mathbf{x}})\outerproduct{\xx}{\xx}\;. (17)

A more detailed derivation of Eq. 16 starting from Eq. 15 can be found in Appendix A.

It must be noted that the above expression is only well defined if ψθ​(𝐱)≠0\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})\neq 0. Through the Monte Carlo estimation of SS and gg, one implicitly assumes that the support of the amplitudes and their gradients is the same. If this is not the case, the expression in Eq. 16 for SS and gg may contain a bias term [14]. We note that g=∇θE​(θ)g=\nabla_{\theta}E(\theta) is precisely the gradient that could have been obtained by direct differentiation of Eq. 12. The matrix SS is commonly called the quantum geometric tensor (QGT) or quantum Fisher information matrix [56, 57, 58] and acts like the metric tensor of the parameter manifold ℳψ\mathcal{M}_{\psi} induced by the distance in the surrounding Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} between un-normalized states defined in Eq. 1. In other words, it can be shown that the following expansion of the quantum fidelity F⁡(⋅,⋅)F(\cdot,\cdot) holds:

F⁡(ψθ+δ​θ,ψθ)=|⟨ψθ+δ​θ|ψθ⟩|2⟨ψθ+δ​θ|ψθ+δ​θ⟩​⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩==1−12​∑μ​νSμ​ν​δ​θμ​δ​θν+⋯.\begin{gathered}F(\psi_{\theta+\delta\theta},\psi_{\theta})=\frac{\left|\innerproduct{\psi_{\theta+ \delta\theta}}{\psi_\theta}\right|^{2}}{\innerproduct{\psi_{\theta+ \delta\theta}}{\psi_{\theta+ \delta\theta}}\innerproduct{\psi_{\theta}}{\psi_{\theta}}}=\\ =1-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mu\nu}S_{\mu\nu}\,\delta\theta^{\mu}\,\delta\theta^{\nu}+\cdots\;.\end{gathered} (18)

The geometrical picture of this optimization procedure then becomes clearer – imaginary time evolution induces a set of trajectories on the Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} connecting different initial states to to the ground state |0⟩\ket{0}. Because we are limited to variational states |ψθ⟩\ket{\psi_\theta}, we project the true trajectory onto the variational manifold ℳψ\mathcal{M}_{\psi}. The states on the projected path |ψθ⁡(τ)⟩\ket{\psi_{\theta(\tau)}} are parametrized by the solution to S​θ˙=−gS\,\dot{\theta}=-g. The choice of how to discretize progress along this projection with sequential parameter updates is left to individual users. A schematic representation of such imaginary time dynamics is given in Fig. 2.

In addition, the SS matrix can be treated in several different approximations:

  • •

    If no approximations are made and a simple Euler integrator is used to discretize the the top level ODE S​θ˙=−gS\,\dot{\theta}=-g, one recovers the quantum natural gradient (QNG) or the stochastic reconfiguration (SR) update rule [57, 56]:

    θ′=θ−δ​τ​S−1​g\theta^{\prime}=\theta-\delta\tau\;S^{-1}g (19)

    We note that more sophisticated integrators can be used as well, usually chosen from the Runge-Kutta (RK) family [59, 60].

  • •

    If SS is instead approximated in block-diagonal form, the Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (KFAC) [61] optimization scheme is recovered. Usually, Sμ​νS_{\mu\nu} is assumed to vanish if μ\mu and ν\nu belong to different layers of the neural network state ψθ\psi_{\theta} but other choices are possible.

  • •

    If we approximate S≈𝟙S\approx\mathbbm{1} in Eq. 19, we obtain stochastic gradient descent (SGD):

    θ′=θ−η​∇θE​(θ),\theta^{\prime}=\theta-\eta\;\nabla_{\theta}E(\theta)\,, (20)

    upon substituting gμ=∂μE⁡(θ)g_{\mu}=\partial_{\mu}E(\theta). We identify δ​τ\delta\tau with the learning rate η\eta.

  • •

    Finally, if we keep S=𝟙S=\mathbbm{1}, we can use any of the popular optimizers from the deep learning literature such as Adam or Adamax [62], RMSProp [63] and others [41].

This hierarchy of increasingly complex optimizers is well-motivated by differential geometry on the manifold ℳψ\mathcal{M}_{\psi}. Quantum natural gradient can be thought of as steepest descent optimization in curved space with metric tensor SS, guaranteeing that the state described by the updated parameters is close in Fubini-Study metric to the initial state. For more insights into geometry on quantum variational manifolds, we refer the interested reader to an excellent review in Ref. [64].

While producing fast convergence and reliable results, the QNG/SR algorithm is sometimes avoided in practice due to the computational overhead for NQS with many parameters. The overhead is coming from the need to solve an P×PP\times P linear system at each step, where PP is the number of parameters. Recently, a group of authors in Ref. [22] introduced a computational trick allowing them to calculate the full preconditioned gradient S−1​gS^{-1}g using only a Ns×NsN_{\text{s}}\times N_{\text{s}} matrix inversion, where NsN_{\text{s}} is the number of samples. This simple trick reduces to exploiting a property of a Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse [65] when evaluating S−1​gS^{-1}g in the finite-sample approximation

S−1​g=(𝒪¯†​𝒪¯)−1​𝒪¯†​ϵ=𝒪¯†​(𝒪¯​𝒪¯†)−1​ϵS^{-1}g=\left(\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}\bar{\mathcal{O}}\right)^{-1}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}\epsilon=\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}\left(\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}\right)^{-1}\epsilon (21)

where 𝒪¯i​μ=⟨𝐱i|⁡(𝒪μ−⟨𝒪μ⟩)​|ψθ⟩/⟨𝐱i|ψθ⟩\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{i\mu}=\bra{\xx_i}\left(\mathcal{O}_{\mu}-\expectationvalue{\OO_\mu}\right)\ket{\psi_\theta}/\innerproduct{\xx_i}{\psi_\theta} and ϵi=EL​(𝐱i)\epsilon_{i}=E_{L}({\mathbf{x}}_{i}). The new algorithm was named minSR and opens the door to QNG on states with ∼106−107\sim 10^{6}-10^{7} parameters.

In summary, the complete program reads:

  1. 1.

    Choose a basis |𝐱⟩\ket{\xx} and define a parameterized wavefunction ψθ​(𝐱)\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}).

  2. 2.

    Approximate averages in Eq. 16 using MC samples and obtain g=∇θEg=\nabla_{\theta}E. (If optimizing using QNG, calculate the preconditioned gradient S−1​gS^{-1}g using an appropriate pseudoinverse S−1S^{-1}.)

  3. 3.

    Update parameters using a gradient-based optimizer.

  4. 4.

    Go to 1. and repeat until convergence.

After convergence has been reached, a measure of the quality of the obtained approximation is necessary. A common choice is the energy variance

Var​E=⟨H2⟩ψθ−⟨H⟩ψθ2{\text{Var}}E=\expectationvalue{H^2}_{\psi_{\theta}}-\expectationvalue{H}^{2}_{\psi_{\theta}} (22)

which vanishes as the true ground state is approached. However, recently, a version of the scaled variance, the V-score, has been proposed by a wide group of authors in Ref. [29] as a more consistent measure of proximity to the ground state across different Hamiltonians and even Hilbert spaces. It is defined as:

V-score=N​Var​E(E−E∞)2,\text{V-score}=\frac{N\;{\text{Var}}E}{(E-E_{\infty})^{2}}\;, (23)

for a system of NN degrees of freedom and an appropriately chosen reference energy E∞E_{\infty}. In essence – lower V-score is better. For a discussion of relevant details and V-scores across different methods and many-body Hamiltonians, we refer the reader to Ref. [29].

II.5 Time-dependent Variational Monte Carlo

The geometrical picture introduced in section II.4 can be readily generalized to projections of other types of trajectories in the Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} onto the variational manifold ℳψ\mathcal{M}_{\psi}. One of the most important developments in that field is unitary evolution in real time. The only difference is replacing τ→i​t\tau\rightarrow i\,t in Eq. 15. Reusing notation from Eq. 16, the relevant equation of motion then becomes S​θ˙=−fS\,\dot{\theta}=-f, where

fμ=2​Im⁡{⟨𝒪μ†​H⟩−⟨𝒪μ†⟩​⟨H⟩}f_{\mu}=2\Im{ \ev{\OO^\dagger_\mu H} - \ev{\OO^\dagger_\mu} \ev{H \vphantom{\OO^\dagger_\mu} } } (24)

and, expectedly, θ˙=dθ/dt\dot{\theta}=\nicefrac{{\differential\theta}}{{\differential t}}. We note that the expression in Eq. 24 is just the imaginary part of the energy gradient gg that was discarded in the case of imaginary time evolution in Eq. 16. This method is called the time-dependent variational Monte Carlo (t-VMC). A good overview of the fundamentals can be found in Refs. [42, 40].

For smaller systems, well-chosen variational states and shorter time horizons, Euler integration can be sufficient to produce good results. However, following the imaginary-time recipe and using a first-order method to step t→t+δ​tt\rightarrow t+\delta t often leads to problems when scaling the algorithm. A part of the solution is to use higher-order and adaptive ODE integrators.

The reason is that the imaginary time evolution in Eq. 14 always has a well-defined limit while evolution in real time does not. In other words, S​θ˙=−gS\dot{\theta}=-g as an ODE is guaranteed to approach a fixed point for a wide range of initial conditions while its real time counterpart S​θ˙=−fS\dot{\theta}=-f is volume-preserving, up to projection errors. This is a direct consequence of the unitarity of the time-evolution operator 𝒰⁡(t)=e−i​H​t\mathcal{U}(t)=e^{-iHt}. As entanglement entropy grows under time evolution, the question becomes when, not if the simulation will become dominated by variational manifold projection errors.

In order delay this cutoff point and make t-VMC useful for larger systems at intermediate times, regularization methods are used when calculating θ˙=−S−1​f\dot{\theta}=-S^{-1}f. Specifically, the SS matrix in Eq. 16 can become singular for trial states with many parameters like deep neural networks, preventing efficient inversion. Authors in Refs. [66, 67, 68] avoid this problem by restricted choices of trial states while authors in Ref. [14] choose to bypass explicit inversion by directly optimizing the overlap between the trial state at time tt and an estimate of the state at time t+δ​tt+\delta t. See Sec. III.3 for a discussion.

Refs. [30, 31] use spectral methods to define a custom pseudoinverse. The approach can be outlined as follows – if SS is diagonalized as S=U​Σ​U†S=U\Sigma U^{\dagger} where Σ=diag​(σ12,…,σP2)\Sigma=\text{diag}(\sigma^{2}_{1},\ldots,\sigma^{2}_{P}) then one can replace

Σμ​ν−1→w⁡(σμ2)σμ2​δμ​νsuch thatlimσ2→0w⁡(σ2)σ2=0,\Sigma^{-1}_{\mu\nu}\rightarrow\frac{w(\sigma^{2}_{\mu})}{\sigma^{2}_{\mu}}\delta_{\mu\nu}\quad\text{such that}\quad\lim_{\sigma^{2}\rightarrow 0}\frac{w(\sigma^{2})}{\sigma^{2}}=0\;, (25)

where δ⋅⁣⋅\delta_{\cdot\cdot} is the Kronecker delta. The function ww can be can be interpreted as spectral weight and good choices usually strongly depend on different ansatz states.

In general, t-VMC regularization and introducing useful inductive biases in trial states is an open field of research.

II.6 Overlap optimization

In some cases such as quantum circuit simulation [34] real-simulation outside the traditional framework of t-VMC [14], an explicit target state |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} is known. This should be contrasted with the traditional VMC setup in Sec. II.4 where the target state is implicit as a ground state of a given hamiltonian operator.

If one can easily evaluate the corresponding wave function ϕ⁡(𝐱)\phi(\mathbf{x}), the following stochastic estimator of the quantum fidelity (introduced in Eq. 18) can be derived:

F⁡(ψ,ϕ)=|⟨ψ|ϕ⟩|2⟨ψ|ψ⟩​⟨ϕ|ϕ⟩=⟨ϕ⁡(𝐱)ψ⁡(𝐱)⟩ψ​⟨ψ⁡(𝐱)ϕ⁡(𝐱)⟩ϕ.F(\psi,\phi)=\frac{\left|\innerproduct{\psi}{\phi}\right|^{2}}{\innerproduct{\psi}{\psi}\innerproduct{\phi}{\phi}}=\expectationvalue{\frac{\phi(\vb{x})}{\psi(\vb{x})}}_{\psi}\expectationvalue{\frac{\psi(\vb{x})}{\phi(\vb{x})}}_{\phi}\;. (26)

The expression in Eq. 26 is manifestly independent of wave function renormalization. In practice, the imaginary part of the fidelity estimator in Eq. 26 is an artefact of finite sampling and is usually discarded.

If working with a parametrized state ψ=ψθ\psi=\psi_{\theta} and a fixed target state ϕ\phi, then minimizing the infidelity 𝒟⁡(ψ,ϕ)=1−F⁡(ψ,ϕ)\mathcal{D}(\psi,\phi)=1-F(\psi,\phi) requires corresponding gradients

∂μ𝒟(ψθ,ϕ)=−F(ψθ,ϕ)∂μlnF(ψθ,ϕ)\partial_{\mu}\mathcal{D}(\psi_{\theta},\phi)=-F(\psi_{\theta},\phi)\;\partial_{\mu}\ln F(\psi_{\theta},\phi) (27)

with

∂μlnF(ψθ,ϕ)=2Re{⟨𝒪μ†⟩ψθ−⟨ϕψθ​𝒪μ†⟩ψθ⟨ϕψθ⟩ψθ}.\partial_{\mu}\ln F(\psi_{\theta},\phi)=2\real\left\{\expectationvalue{ \OO^\dagger_\mu}_{\psi_{\theta}}-\frac{\expectationvalue{ \frac{\phi}{\psi_\theta} \OO^\dagger_\mu}_{\psi_{\theta}}}{\expectationvalue{\frac{\phi}{\psi_\theta}}_{\psi_{\theta}}}\right\}\;. (28)

As an alternative to direct computation, we note that the expression for infidelity in Eq. 26 can be rewritten as an expectation value of an effective Hamiltonian:

𝒟⁡(ψθ,ϕ)=⟨ψθ|Heffϕ|ψθ⟩⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩​with​Heffϕ=𝟙−|ϕ⟩⟨ϕ|⟨ϕ|ϕ⟩.\mathcal{D}(\psi_{\theta},\phi)=\frac{\expectationvalue{H ^\phi_\text{eff}}{\psi_\theta}}{\innerproduct{\psi_\theta}{\psi_\theta}}\;\;\text{with}\;\;H^{\phi}_{\text{eff}}=\mathbbm{1}-\frac{\outerproduct{\phi}{\phi}}{\innerproduct{\phi}{\phi}}\;. (29)

Using the effective Hamiltonian from Eq. 29 to compute gradients defined in Eq. 16 recovers the expression in Eq. 28 and makes using the SR optimizer a natural choice in this case as well.

II.7 Maximum likelihood estimation

In contrast to the fidelity optimization case where the target state amplitudes ϕ⁡(𝐱)\phi({\mathbf{x}}) are known, we now focus on the task of finding an approximate representation |ψθ⟩|\psi_{\theta}\rangle to a target state |ϕ⟩|\phi\rangle without direct access to its amplitudes ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x). Here we only have access to a training set of basis states 𝒯={𝐱[b]\mathcal{T}=\{{\mathbf{x}}^{[b]} } on different bases [b][b] sampled according to |⟨𝐱[b]|​|ϕ⟩|2\left|\bra{ \xx^{[b]}}\ket{ \phi}\right|^{2}. Here the states |𝐱[b]⟩\ket*{\xx^{[b]}} are obtained as:

|𝐱[b]⟩=U[b]​|𝐱⟩,\ket*{\xx^{[b]}}=U^{[b]}\ket{\xx}, (30)

with U[b]U^{[b]} the change of basis unitary that transforms {|𝐱⟩}↦{|𝐱[b]⟩}\{\ket{\xx}\}\mapsto\left\{\ket*{\xx^{[b]}}\right\}. This is the typical problem encountered in quantum state tomography or quantum state reconstruction, where we have access to projective measurements on different bases on a quantum experiment, and we seek to reconstruct the underlying quantum state. Within the umbrella of machine learning, this can be understood as a density estimation task. As such, the natural choice to find |ψθ⟩\ket{\psi_\theta} is the optimization, with respect to θ\theta of the KL divergence [41] between the distributions defined by |⟨𝐱[b]|​|ϕ⟩|2\left|\bra*{ \xx^{[b]}}\ket{ \phi}\right|^{2} and |⟨𝐱[b]|​|ψθ⟩|2\left|\bra*{ \xx^{[b]}}\ket{ \psi_\theta}\right|^{2}:

𝒟KL​(|ϕ|2∥|ψθ|2)=∑b∑𝐱[b]|ϕ¯​(𝐱[b])|2​ln⁡|ϕ¯​(𝐱[b])|2|ψ¯θ​(𝐱[b])|2.\mathcal{D}_{\textrm{KL}}\left(|\phi|^{2}\middle\||\psi_{\theta}|^{2}\right)=\sum_{b}\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}^{[b]}}|\bar{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}^{[b]})|^{2}\ln\frac{|\bar{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}^{[b]})|^{2}}{|\bar{\psi}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}^{[b]})|^{2}}. (31)

|ϕ¯⟩\ket*{\bar{\phi}} and |ψ¯θ⟩\ket*{\bar{\psi}_\theta} label the explicitly normalized counterparts to |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} and |ψθ⟩\ket{\psi_\theta}. In the above expression, the sum over bb runs over all (exponentially-many) basis choices, and the sum over all (exponentially-many) elements of each basis 𝐱[b]{\mathbf{x}}^{[b]}. Different bases bb are required to be able to capture the phase structure of the target state. An unbiased estimator can be obtained as:

𝒟KL​(|ϕ|2∥|ψθ|2)≈1|𝒯|​∑𝐱[b]∈𝒯ln⁡|ϕ¯​(𝐱[b])|2|ψ¯θ​(𝐱[b])|2.\mathcal{D}_{\textrm{KL}}\left(|\phi|^{2}\middle\||\psi_{\theta}|^{2}\right)\approx\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}^{[b]}\in\mathcal{T}}\ln\frac{|\bar{\phi}({\mathbf{x}}^{[b]})|^{2}}{|\bar{\psi}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}^{[b]})|^{2}}. (32)

The gradients of the empirical cost function are given by:

∂θ𝒟KL​(|ϕ|2∥|ψθ|2)≈1NN​∑i=1NN∂θln⁡|ψθ​(𝐱i)|2−1|𝒯|​∑𝐱[b]∈𝒯∂θln⁡|ψθ​(𝐱[b])|2.\begin{gathered}\partial_{\theta}\mathcal{D}_{\textrm{KL}}\left(|\phi|^{2}\middle\||\psi_{\theta}|^{2}\right)\approx\\ \frac{1}{N_{\textrm{N}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\textrm{N}}}\partial_{\theta}\ln|\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})|^{2}-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}^{[b]}\in\mathcal{T}}\partial_{\theta}\ln|\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}^{[b]})|^{2}.\end{gathered} (33)

The first term, proportional to 1/NN1/N_{\textrm{N}}, is the empirical average of the gradient of the normalization factor, evaluated over NNN_{\textrm{N}} samples 𝐱i{\mathbf{x}}_{i} collected from |ψθ|2|\psi_{\theta}|^{2}. The second term contains the gradient of the wave function amplitudes evaluated at basis states sampled according to the target state. Recall that:

ψθ​(𝐱[b])=∑𝐱U𝐱,𝐱[b][b]​ψθ​(𝐱).\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}^{[b]})=\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}}U^{[b]}_{{\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{[b]}}\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}). (34)

We immediately recognize that in order for the KL optimization to be computationally efficient, the chosen bases that form the training set must satisfy that U[b]U^{[b]} is k−localk-\textrm{local}, so ψθ​(𝐱[b])\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}^{[b]}) can be efficiently evaluated. This technique was introduced in Ref. [35], adapted to a density-matrix formulation in Ref. [69], and applied to real experimental data in Ref. [70].

II.8 Symmetries

The imposition of discrete symmetries in NQS is an active field of research. Consider the case where the Hamiltonian of the system is invariant under the action of set of symmetry operations 𝒮={T}\mathcal{S}=\{T\}. Some examples of TT symmetry operations include translation, rotation or mirror symmetries or combinations thereof. The wave function amplitudes of the eigenstates of the Hamiltonian must satisfy the symmetry property:

ψ⁡(T⁡(𝐱))=χT​ψ​(𝐱),\psi(T({\mathbf{x}}))=\chi_{T}\psi({\mathbf{x}}), (35)

for all T∈𝒮T\in\mathcal{S}. χT\chi_{T} is the character of the symmetry operation TT, and is a phase factor. The value of χT\chi_{T} depends on the symmetry sector that |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle belongs to.

The imposition of the symmetry requirements in Eq. 35 in the parametric model ψθS\psi^{\text{S}}_{\theta} can be achieved by the direct symmetrization of the trial state amplitudes of a non-symmetric ansatz [71]:

ψθS​(𝐱)=∑T∈𝒮χT​ψθ​(T−1​(𝐱)).\psi^{\text{S}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})=\sum_{T\in\mathcal{S}}\chi_{T}\;\psi_{\theta}\left(T^{-1}({\mathbf{x}})\right). (36)

The direct symmetrization approach suffers from an increased computational cost of a factor of |𝒮||\mathcal{S}| every time a wave function amplitude or gradient needs to be evaluated. This computational overhead affects the estimation of expectation values as well as the sampling procedure. Alternatively, symmetry projections can be applied to a non-symmetric state after it has been optimized, obtaining improvements in the variational energy in the context of ground-state calculations [26]. The use of symmetry-equivariant neural networks like traditional convolutional neural networks [19, 21, 72], their generalization to group-convolutions [73] or graph convolutional networks [20] also allow to bypass the explicit evaluation of ψθ​(T​(𝐱))\psi_{\theta}(T({\mathbf{x}})) for all T∈𝒮T\in\mathcal{S} every time the variational state is symmetrized.

For ground state calculations, it is desirable to identify the symmetry sector that the ground state belongs to, to directly use the right characters for the symmetry operations. If this is not possible, separate ground state calculations must be carried projecting to all possible symmetry subspaces [71]. Amongst all optimized states on different subspaces, the ground state is identified with the one that has the lowest energy, as per the variational principle.

In the particular case where χT=1\chi_{T}=1 for all T∈𝒮T\in\mathcal{S}, the action of any non linear function ff on ∑T∈𝒮ψθ​(T−1​(𝐱))\sum_{T\in\mathcal{S}}\psi_{\theta}\left(T^{-1}({\mathbf{x}})\right) yields a wave function ansatz that respects the symmetries of the Hamiltonian. Ref. [21] explores different functional choices for ff for systems of interacting spins.

In some cases it is useful to fix the character a priori to obtain excited states from the direct optimization of the expectation value of the Hamiltonian [74]. If the target excited state is know to belong to a different symmetry sector to the ground state, the character of the symmetry can be fixed to the character corresponding to the symmetry subspace where the symmetries live. Consequently, the variational state is forced to live in a variational manifold that is not connected to the ground state.

It is also possible to impose non-Abelian anyonic symmetries in the context of NQS [75, 76]. This is however requires a more involved technique.

It has been reported in numerous works that symmetry projections always improve the accuracy of the variational wave function.

III Applications

III.1 Ground-state properties of spin systems

III.1.1 Hamiltonians

Systems of interacting spins are the first class of many-body problems that were tackled by NQS [3]. Systems of spins provide with a platform to study the fundamental properties of NQS and compare their expressive power against other variational methods, like tensor network methods. A general interacting spin Hamiltonian can be written as:

H=∑i​jJi​j​(𝝈i⊤​C​𝝈j)−∑i𝝈i⊤​𝒃i,H=\sum_{ij}J_{ij}\left(\bm{\sigma}_{i}^{\top}C\bm{\sigma}_{j}\right)-\sum_{i}\bm{\sigma}^{\top}_{i}\bm{b}_{i}, (37)

𝝈i⊤=(σix,σiy,σiz)\bm{\sigma}_{i}^{\top}=(\sigma^{x}_{i},\sigma^{y}_{i},\sigma^{z}_{i}) is the row-vector of Pauli operators acting on spin ii. Ji​jJ_{ij} represents the interaction strength between spins ii and jj. Ji​j>0J_{ij}>0 (Ji​j<0J_{ij}<0) corresponds to antiferromagnetic (ferromagnetic interactions). CC is a 3×33\times 3 positive semidefinite matrix that characterizes the anisotropy of the interaction. 𝒃i\bm{b}_{i} is a three-dimensional vector with the components of an external field applied to spin ii. Many spin Hamiltonians can be written in this form, including the Ising, Heisenberg and J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} models on different geometries.

III.1.2 Feedforward variational models

One of the most widely used neural-network parametrizations for systems of spins is the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM). The output of the RBM can be interpreted as the output of the Boltzmann distribution of a set of classical spins (input variables) that have Ising-like interactions with a collection of HH hidden spins, and optionally magnetic fields. Alternatively, the RBM can be seen as a two-layer perceptron with a very particular activation function. The strengths of the interactions and magnetic fields represent the weights 𝒘\bm{w} and biases 𝒂\bm{a} and 𝒃\bm{b} respectively of the neural network. Given the input row vector 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}, the RBM produces the output:

ψθ​(𝐱)=e𝐱⋅𝒂​∏i=1H2​cosh⁡[(𝐱⋅𝒘+𝒃)i].\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})=e^{{\mathbf{x}}\cdot\bm{a}}\prod_{i=1}^{H}2\cosh\left[({\mathbf{x}}\cdot\bm{w}+\bm{b})_{i}\right]. (38)

The number of hidden units HH controls the expressive power of the ansatz. Real variational parameters 𝒘\bm{w}, 𝒂\bm{a} and 𝒃\bm{b} make ψθ​(𝐱)\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}) to be real positive semidefinite, thus not being able to capture the intricate sign structures of many-body wave functions. The promotion of 𝒘\bm{w}, 𝒂\bm{a} and 𝒃\bm{b} to complex variables allows to capture the phases of the target state [3]. The expressive power of the RBM can be further improved by allowing the input vector 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} to contain both the sampled spin configuration along the quantization axis, as well as correlation functions (quadratic forms) of the spin configurations [77]. This is known as the correlation enhanced RBM. We also note that closely related feedforward models have been used for bosonic systems in Refs. [78, 79, 80].

Deeper and more involved neural network architectures, which in some cases include symmetry projections, convolutions and graph convolutions have been used to study challenging spin Hamiltonians like the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model in square [19, 20, 21, 22], triangular, honeycomb and Kagome lattices [20], or the Heisenberg model in the Pyrochlore lattice [23].

III.1.3 Auto-regressive recurrent models

The field saw an important advancement with the introduction of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to approximately represent the ground state of spin Hamiltonians [54, 81, 82]. The RNN-based parametrization of a quantum state is defined by:

ψθ​(𝐱)=Pθ​(𝐱)​ei​ϕθ​(𝐱),\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})=\sqrt{P_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})}\;e^{i\phi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})}, (39)

where ϕθ​(𝐱)\phi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}) is a parametric phase factor (which can be represented by a feedforward model) and Pθ​(𝐱)P_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}) is an auto-regressive distribution model spanned by the chain rule of probabilities (see Eq. 11), where each conditional probability is normalized. Recurrent neural networks are a good candidate to parametrize the chain of conditionals needed to reconstruct PθP_{\theta} as shown in Fig. 4. This class of models supports auto-regressive sampling and therefore is capable of producing perfect uncorrelated samples, as discussed in Sec. II.3.2.

RNN architectures have successfully described physical properties of various spin models on different lattice geometries [83, 54, 84, 85, 86] as well as agreement with experimental observations of two-dimensional Rydberg atom array dynamics [87].

An open challenge for RNN-based parametrizations with auto-regressive sampling is the imposition of U⁡(1)U(1)-like symmetries, such as magnetization of particle number conservation [88, 83, 54, 84, 89, 81, 90].

III.1.4 Expressive power, entanglement entropy and connections to tensor networks

The understanding of the classes of states that can be efficiently11 1 By efficiently we mean with an amount of computational resources that scales polynomially with the system size represented by NQS is of imperative relevance to asses the utility of this class of trial states.

In the space of feedforward architectures, it has been shown that the RBM can efficiently represents quantum states with volume-law entanglement entropy [91]. This result has been generalized to deep RNN and CNN architectures, showing that the deed architectures are capable of supporting volume-law scaling polynomially more efficiently than the RBM. These results suggest that deep architectures provide an advantage over shallow architectures to represent quantum states. Complexity-theory arguments support these statements [7]. Ref. [7] argues that most physical quantum states can be represented by deep neural networks, while shallow architectures may not be able to efficiently represent some classes of physical quantum states. This means that while RBMs are capable of representing families of states with entanglement that follows a volume-law scaling, some of those states may not be relevant in the context of the simulation of physical systems.

By simply considering entanglement-entropy arguments, it might appear that NQS are more expressive that MPSs, since the MPS can only efficiently represent states whose entanglement follows an area-law [13]. This is however not the right evaluation in general, since there are physical quantum states that are not accessible to shallow NQS that can be represented by an MPS [7, 92, 93]. With the goal of finding the overlapping family of quantum states that can be both represented by TN states and NQS states, a body of work is centered around the search of exact mappings between TNs and NQS. Ref. [8] provides an injective map between locally-interacting RBMs (most weights 𝒘\bm{w} set to zero) and an MPS. Ref. [8] also show that some MPSs can be exactly mapped into a locally-interacting RBM. However, this work does not provide a recipe to exactly map an arbitrary MPS to a RBM.

The authors of Ref. [9] follow a different approach to construct mappings between TNs and NNs. An algorithm is provided to construct NN layers that efficiently perform tensor contractions. Therefore, a deep NN can be constructed to exactly represent an efficiently contractable TN, of course including the MPS. It was also found that the number of NN weights required for this mapping closely matches the contraction complexity of the TN. This results implies that deep NQS have strictly the same or more expressive power than efficiently contractable TNs. For example, any MPS can be exactly mapped into a deep NN whose total number of parameters grows polynomially with the bond dimension of the MPS, and whose depth grows logarithmically with the system size [9]. Given that deep NQS can represent states with entropy that follows a volume-law scaling and MPS cannot, this implies that MPS with polynomially-scaling bond dimension are s strict subset of deep NQS. Interestingly, these results can be generalized to RNNs [10].

A word of caution.–

The results on the expressive power of NQS are really promising, and may even male the reader wonder why to use TN approaches like the DMRG at all if NQS provide a more expressive representation of quantum states. However, we would like to note that TN approaches like the DMRG pose two substantial advantages over NQS approaches. The first one is that some classes of TNs can be efficiently contracted, thus not requiring stochastic noisy estimates of expectation values. The second advantage is that some TN methods like the DMRG do not rely on gradient-based optimization techniques to optimize the parameters of the variational states. The reliance of NQS in gradient-based approaches make their accuracy strongly reliant on having a non-pathological variational energy landscape. However, at the time, the properties and topology of the variational energy landscape for NQS parametrizations is not well understood. Further systematic investigations are required to characterize the optimization dynamics of NQS.

III.2 Ground-state properties of fermionic systems

III.2.1 Hamiltonians

Neural quantum states have been extensively employed to study systems of interacting electrons. The Hamiltonian for a system of NN interacting electrons in the presence of NnucN_{\text{nuc}} atomic nuclei, in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation form reads:

H=−12∑n𝐏n2+∑n<m1|𝐫n−𝐫m|−∑n,AZA|𝐫n−𝐑A|+∑A<BZA​ZB|𝐑A−𝐑B|.\begin{split}H&=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n}\mathbf{P}_{n}^{2}+\sum_{n<m}\frac{1}{\left|\mathbf{r}_{n}-\mathbf{r}_{m}\right|}\\ &-\sum_{n,A}\frac{Z_{A}}{\left|\mathbf{r}_{n}-\mathbf{R}_{A}\right|}+\sum_{A<B}\frac{Z_{A}Z_{B}}{\left|\mathbf{R}_{A}-\mathbf{R}_{B}\right|}.\end{split} (40)

Note that atomic units have been used. In the equation above lowercase indices n,mn,\;m label electronic degrees of freedom while uppercase indices A,BA,\;B label nuclear degrees of freedom. 𝑷n\bm{P}_{n} and 𝒓n\bm{r}_{n} are the linear momentum and position operators the electrons. 𝑹A\bm{R}_{A} labels the classical variable associated to the position of the atomic nuclei. NQS can be used directly in the continuum description of the problem [94, 27, 95, 28, 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101] . This is also known as the first quantization approach.

It must also be noted that other fermionic many-body Hamiltonians have been addressed using neural quantum states. In particular, an area that is receiving increasing interest is the use of NQS to obtain the ground state properties of systems of interacting nucleons [102, 103, 104, 105, 106].

The Hamiltonian in Eq. 40 is defined on a Hilbert space with an uncountable number of degrees of freedom. The same Hilbert space can be projected onto a truncated basis-set defined by a countable number NorbN_{\textrm{orb}} of orthonormal single-particle basis states or orbitals: {|ϕp⟩:p=1,…,Norb}\left\{\ket{\phi_p}\;:\;p=1,\ldots,N_{\textrm{orb}}\right\}. The associated creation operators for the set of orbitals is defined by |ϕp⟩=ap†​|∅⟩\ket{\phi_p}=a^{\dagger}_{p}\ket{\varnothing}.

Since fermions live in the subspace of completely anti-symmetric states with NN-particles, a suitable basis is obtained from explicitly anti-symmetrized products of single-particle basis states:

|ϕp1​…​ϕpn⟩=ap1†​…​apN†​|∅⟩==1N!​∑Π∈SNξ⁡(Π)​|ϕΠ1⟩⊗…⊗|ϕΠN⟩,\begin{gathered}\ket{\phi_{p_1}\hdots\phi_{p_n} }=a^{\dagger}_{p_{1}}\ldots a^{\dagger}_{p_{N}}\ket{\varnothing}=\\ =\frac{1}{\sqrt{N!}}\sum_{\Pi\in\textrm{S}_{N}}\xi(\Pi)\ket{\phi_{\Pi_1}}\otimes\ldots\otimes\ket{\phi_{\Pi_N}},\end{gathered} (41)

where SN\textrm{S}_{N} is the symmetric group of NN elements and Π\Pi labels a permutations of the {p1,…,pN}\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}\} indices whose sign is given by ξ⁡(Π)\xi(\Pi). In this truncated representation of the many-body Hilbert space the Hamiltonian in 40 can be written in terms of creation and annihilation operators:

H=∑p​qσhp​q​cp​σ†​cq​σ+∑p​q​r​sσ​τhp​q​r​s2​cp​σ†​cq​τ†​cs​τ​cr​σ\begin{gathered}H=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}pq\\ \sigma\end{subarray}}h_{pq}c^{\dagger}_{p\sigma}c_{q\sigma}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}pqrs\\ \sigma\tau\end{subarray}}\frac{h_{pqrs}}{2}c^{\dagger}_{p\sigma}c^{\dagger}_{q\tau}c_{s\tau}c_{r\sigma}\end{gathered} (42)

where σ,τ∈{↑,↓}\sigma,\tau\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\} and hp​qh_{pq} and hp​q​r​sh_{pqrs} are the one- and two-body matrix elements. Their values depends on the choice of single-particle orbitals and can be extracted from quantum chemistry packages [107, 108, 109]. The interacting-electron Hamiltonian is number and magnetization preserving as well as S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric. Note that the indices p,q,r,sp,q,r,s run from 11 to NorbN_{\textrm{orb}}. Consequently, the number of terms in the Hamiltonian scales as 𝒪⁡((Norb)4)\mathcal{O}\left((N_{\textrm{orb}})^{4}\right). The asymptotic scaling on the number of terms in the Hamiltonian is multiplied to the asymptotic scaling of the wave function evaluation. Therefore, the direct study of the interacting electron Hamiltonian in second quantization becomes computationally expensive rapidly. NQS have also been extensively used to study systems of interacting electrons on a discrete basis set [110, 111, 112, 113, 114, 115, 116, 89, 117, 118, 24, 72, 25, 26, 119, 11, 88].

Hamiltonians in Eqs. 40 and 42 are referred to as ab-initio Hamiltonians. It is at this point where physically-motivated approximations can be implemented to reduce the number of terms in the two-body part of the Hamiltonian. Under reasonable assumptions of locality of tightly bound electrons in periodic arrangements of atoms led Hubbard [120] to derive a simplified interacting electron Hamiltonian. The simplest version of the Hubbard Hamiltonian considers only a single orbital per atom (single-band), one-body processes between adjacent atoms and interaction processes only between electrons in the same atom, yielding the Hamiltonian

H=−t∑⟨p,q⟩,σ(cp​σ†cq​σ+cq​σ†cp​σ)+U∑pnp↑np↓,H=-t\sum_{\expectationvalue{p, q},\sigma}\left(c^{\dagger}_{p\sigma}c_{q\sigma}+c^{\dagger}_{q\sigma}c_{p\sigma}\right)+U\sum_{p}n_{p\uparrow}n_{p\downarrow}, (43)

where tt is the hopping amplitude and UU is the onsite interaction strength. The Hubbard model provides a minimal description of locally interacting electrons hopping between adjacent sites of a given lattice. Despite its simple appearance, the complete understanding of its ground-state properties is still a very active field of research [121, 122, 123, 124, 125].

III.2.2 Symmetrization considerations

Fermionic systems pose a unique challenge due to their particle statistics. As a consequence, the creation and annihilation operators satisfy the commutation relations:

{ap,aq}={ap†,aq†}=0;and{ap,aq†}=δp​q.\left\{a_{p},a_{q}\right\}=\left\{a^{\dagger}_{p},a^{\dagger}_{q}\right\}=0\,;\quad\text{and}\quad\left\{a_{p},a^{\dagger}_{q}\right\}=\delta_{pq}\,. (44)

A consequence of the above commutation relations is that ap2=(ap†)2=0a_{p}^{2}=\left(a^{\dagger}_{p}\right)^{2}=0 (Pauli’s exclusion principle).

The basis of the subspace of completely anti-symmetric states can be spanned in terms of either canonically-ordered or non-canonically-states. This has an impact on the symmetry properties of the wave function amplitudes ψθ​(𝐱)\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}).

First consider the case where the Hilbert space is spanned in terms of non-canonically-ordered states:

{|ϕp1​…​ϕpN⟩:pi=1,…,M}.\{\ket{\phi_{p_1} \hdots\phi_{p_N}}\>:\>p_{i}=1,\ldots,M\}. (45)

From now on the symbol 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} represents the index set p1,…,pNp_{1},\ldots,p_{N} and |𝐱⟩:=|ϕp1​…​ϕpN⟩\ket{\xx}:=\ket{\phi_{p_1} \hdots\phi_{p_N}}. The basis expansion in terms of non-canonically-ordered states is highly redundant since:

|𝐱⟩=ξ⁡(Π)​|Π⁡(𝐱)⟩\ket{\xx}=\xi(\Pi)\ket{\Pi(\xx)} (46)

for all Π∈SN\Pi\in\text{S}_{N}, and |SN|=N!|\text{S}_{N}|=N!. This is a consequence of the anti-commutation relations of the creation operators. This is reflected in the 1/N!1/N! prefactor in the resolution of the identity:

𝟙=1N!​∑𝐱|𝐱⟩⟨𝐱|.\mathbbm{1}=\frac{1}{N!}\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\outerproduct{\xx}{\xx}. (47)

A direct consequence of Eq. 46 is that the wave function amplitudes must satisfy:

ψθ​(𝐱)=ξ⁡(Π)​ψθ​(Π⁡(𝐱))\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})=\xi(\Pi)\psi_{\theta}(\Pi({\mathbf{x}})) (48)

for all Π∈SN\Pi\in\text{S}_{N}. Wave function amplitudes are anti-symmetric functions of the orbital labels.

Alternatively, the subspace of completely anti-symmetric states can be spanned in terms of canonically-ordered states {|  ⟩}\{\ket{\encircled{\xx}}\}, where we choose the ordering where the orbitals
