\hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}} labels the permutation that brings an arbitrary electronic configuration 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} to its ordered counterpart .

Since there is a on-to-one map between canonically-ordered configurations and the occupancy of the orbitals nn, variational wave functions spanned in terms of canonically-ordered states are commonly taken to be functions of the orbital occupancies ψθ:n↦ℂ\psi_{\theta}:n\mapsto\mathbb{C}.

In the canonically-ordered representation, every-time that an operator QQ (which is to be written in terms of creation and annihilation operator) acts on a basis state, the resulting states must be brought back to their canonically-ordered form, which is accomplished by computing the sign of the permutation of the transformations. The book-keeping of signs of permutations can be conceptualized by the Jordan-Wigner mapping [126]. However, in practice it is more efficient to keep track of the signs by hand.

The variational states used to describe systems of interacting fermions can be divided into two groups: non-determinant- and determinant-based parametrizations. Traditionally, non-determinant-based parametrizations are employed when the Hilbert space is spanned in terms of canonically-ordered states [110, 111, 112, 115, 113, 114, 89, 116, 88], while determinant-based parametrizations are employed when the Hilbert space is spanned by non-canonically-order states [24, 72, 105, 106, 26, 27, 28, 25]. There are however exceptions [117, 119].

III.2.3 Non-determinant-based parametrizations

Non-determinant, neural-network-based parametrizations were first introduced to tackle the electronic structure properties of small molecules described by minimal basis sets [110, 111, 112, 115]. Following the tradition in the field, most of this works employed the RBM as the trial wave function. The RBM ansatz has also been employed to study the ground-state properties of solids, including hydrogen chains and three-dimensional LiH in their minimal basis sets, as well as graphene described by a correlation-consistent basis set [113]. The work in Ref. [113] also included Krylov susbpace methods to accurately reconstruct the spectra of excitations of these systems. Other classes of machine learning models based on Gaussian processes have also been proven successful in tackling molecular systems on a basis set [114].

RNNs have also been used to describe the ground-state properties of the electronic degrees of freedom of molecules [89, 116], as well as lattice models [88]. Ref. [88] also provides a path to computing excitations using NQS-based parameterizations. The main advantage behind the use of RNNs as opposed to feedforward neural networks is that, thanks to the auto-regressive sampling support, they produce uncorrelated samples. This may be of great relevance in the description of molecular systems projected on a basis set, since there are some basis choices where the wave function is concentrated around a small number of electronic configurations, while the amplitude of the remaining configurations decays exponentially. Thus, posing a challenge for Markov-Chain-based samplers.

Lattice models, like the Hubbard model have also been addressed by deep NQS [117]. Alternative fermion-to-spin mappings can be used in this context [118].

III.2.4 Determinant-based parametrizations.

Slater determinant.–

The determinant-based parametrizations use Slater determinant states as a starting point, and add correlations to them. The Slater determinant state |ψSD⟩\ket{\psi_\text{SD}} for a system with NN particles is obtained by populating NN variational orbitals:

|ψSD⟩=φ1†​…​φN†​|∅⟩,\ket{\psi_\text{SD}}=\varphi^{\dagger}_{1}\ldots\varphi^{\dagger}_{N}\ket{\varnothing}, (50)

where φα†=∑pΦp,α​ap†\varphi^{\dagger}_{\alpha}=\sum_{p}\Phi_{p,\alpha}a^{\dagger}_{p}. The rectangular matrix Φ∈ℂM×N\Phi\in\mathbb{C}^{M\times N} controls the definition of the variational orbitals, and its matrix elements are the variational parameters. The wave function amplitudes of the Slater determinant are given by:

ψSD​(𝐱)=⟨𝐱|​|ψSD⟩=det⁡[Φp1,1…Φp1,N⋱ΦpN,1…ΦpN,N].\psi_{\text{SD}}({\mathbf{x}})=\bra{\xx}\ket{\psi_\text{SD}}=\det\begin{bmatrix}\Phi_{p_{1},1}&\ldots&\Phi_{p_{1},N}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \Phi_{p_{N},1}&\ldots&\Phi_{p_{N},N}\\ \end{bmatrix}. (51)

Note that the exchange of two of the indices in 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} swaps two rows in the determinant, thus making the amplitudes anti-symmetric, as required by Eq. 48. Also note that, the same variational state can be used even when the Hilbert space is spanned in terms of canonically-ordered states. In this case, one just had to replace 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} by in Eq. 51. When working in the continuum the Slater determinant is obtained by replacing the columns in Φ\Phi (which can be understood as a lookup table of single-particle orbital amplitudes) by functions that depend on the coordinate of one particle Φα​(𝐱i)\Phi_{\alpha}({\mathbf{x}}_{i}). The Slater determinant is the anti-symmetrization of a product state and therefore is incapable of capturing electronic correlations.

Jastrow-like correlation factors.–

Correlations can be achieved by the multiplication of a permutation-symmetric correlation factor 𝒮\mathcal{S} (Jastrow factor [127]):

ψθ​(𝐱)=ψSD​(𝐱)​𝒮θ​(𝐱)\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})=\psi_{\text{SD}}({\mathbf{x}})\mathcal{S}_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}) (52)

The Jastrow factor can be parametrized by a neural network. When working on a basis-set, the Jastrow factor is typically taken to be a function of the fermionic mode occupancies: 𝒮:n↦ℂ\mathcal{S}:n\mapsto\mathbb{C}, thus becoming automatically symmetric. The use of neural-network correlation factors was first introduced in Ref. [24], where a RBM with real parameters was used as a correlation factor on top of a pairing wave function, focusing on the ground-state properties of the Hubbard model in square geometries. The RBM of real parameters can only produce positive semidefinite outputs. Consequently, the Jastrow factor in Ref. [24] can only correct the amplitudes of the reference anti-symmetric state. The generalization of this idea to more complex neural-network architectures was introduced in Ref. [72], where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is parametrized by the product of two CNN with skip connections. The first one, producing a positive semidefinite output is in charge of correcting the amplitudes of the reference Slater determinant, while the second one produces an output in the interval (−1,1)(-1,1), in charge of altering the nodal structure of the reference state. This ansatz is universal in the description of wave functions of interacting systems of fermions described by a countable number of degrees of freedom 22 2 In the context of NQS for fermionic systems, universal representation claims are based on lookup-table arguments, thus not providing any practical information on the classes of states that can be represented by these ansatze.. Ref. [72] focuses on the study of the ground-state phase diagram of spin-polarized lattice fermions. Uncorrelated sampling can also be achieved with Slater-Jastrow functional forms, where the Jastrow factors are given by RNNs [128]. Neural network Jastrow factors have also been extensively used to study systems of interacting nucleons [105, 106].

Backflow correlations.–

Alternatively, correlations can be incorporated in Slater determinants through Backflow transformations [42, 129, 130, 131, 132, 133]. In the continuum representation of the problem this involves replacing the single-particle coordinates that are the inputs to the orbitals that enter the determinant: Φα​(𝐱i)→Φα​(𝐱¯i)\Phi_{\alpha}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})\rightarrow\Phi_{\alpha}(\bar{{\mathbf{x}}}_{i}), where 𝐱¯\bar{{\mathbf{x}}} is referred to as backflow coordinates:

Bθ:𝐱↦𝐱¯,B_{\theta}:{\mathbf{x}}\mapsto\bar{{\mathbf{x}}}, (53)

where BθB_{\theta} is a parametric function that maps the electron coordinates to the backflow coordinates. For the determinant to maintain its ant-symmetry properties, the function BθB_{\theta} is required to be permutation-equivariant. Ref. [94] represented the backflow transformation using neural-network-like functional forms. Non-linear and parametrized backflow transformations are composed and applied to the input electron coordinates. This goes by the name of iterative backflow. Later, Refs. [27, 95], introduced the FermiNet neural network architecture to parametrize BθB_{\theta}. The FermiNet architecture is agnostic to known properties that the wave function must satisfy, like the Kato cusp conditions [134], and is expected to learn to reproduce the correct behaviour. It has been empirically demonstrated that the FermiNet ansatz can achieve great levels of accuracy in the description of the ground state properties of molecular systems. The PauliNet [28] wave function ansatz is also based on the parametrization of the backflow transformation using neural networks, but exactly incorporates the Kato cusp conditions. The PauliNet ansatz also considers a Jastrow-like factor to account for the electron-electron cusp conditions. Like the FermiNet ansatz, the PauliNet variational state achieves great levels of accuracy in molecular systems. The PauliNet ansatz has also been proven successful to obtain low-laying exited states in molecules [96], by optimizing the expectation value of the Hamiltonian with an overlap penalty to the ground states. More recently, a novel approach exploits the properties of determinants to ensure linear independence of a number of excited states [135], allowing for the simultaneous search of a number of excited states above the ground state. Motivated by the recent success of large language models, which strongly rely on attention mechanisms, self-attention parametrizations have been employed to parametrize the backflow transformation BθB_{\theta} [97]. Since self attention mechanisms in essence represent a parametrized two-point correlation function, the idea of using self-attention mechanisms to parametrize wave functions can be seen as the generalization of the correlation-enhanced NQS introduced in Ref. [77].

All of the previously mentioned studies focus on molecular systems. Recently, the neural-network parametrization of backflow transformations has been applied to periodic systems, including the two-dimensional electron gas [98], the three-dimensional electron gas [99], the three-dimensional Fermi gas [100, 101] and Moire systems [136].

The backflow parametrizations of fermionic wave functions constitute a universal wave function approximator for continuous degrees of freedom [27].

When working on a basis set, the backflow wave function is obtained by allowing the matrix elements of Φ\Phi to be configuration-dependent [137, 138]:

ΦBF:𝐱↦ℂM×N,\Phi_{\text{BF}}:{\mathbf{x}}\mapsto\mathbb{C}^{M\times N}, (54)

where ΦBF\Phi_{\text{BF}} is required to be symmetric with respect to permutations in 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}, often-times being a function of the fermionic mode occupancies. The use of neural networks to parametrize ΦBF\Phi_{\text{BF}} to study lattice models was introduced in Ref. [25], achieving great levels of accuracy in the ground state properties of the Hubbard model on a range of geometries. Backflow wave functions are also a universal wave function approximator for fermionic systems with a countable number of degrees of freedom [25].

Neural-network constrained hidden fermion determinant states.–

Traditional hidden particle approaches have allowed to obtain significant insight on the properties of fermionic lattice models like the Hubbard model and its variants like the t−Jt-J model [139, 140, 141, 142, 143, 144, 145, 146, 147, 148, 149, 150, 151, 152, 153, 154, 155, 156, 157]. Hidden particle approaches are rooted on the augmentation of the Hilbert space of the problem by the addition of extra degrees of freedom, which can be of spin, bosonic or fermionic nature. In the augmented Hilbert space, a mean-field theory can be considered. A subsequent projection to a subspace of the augmented Hilbert space identified with the physical degrees of freedom allows to recover a description of the correlations in the system. In the traditional formulation, the characteristics of the added degrees of freedom and the projection are chosen based on the expected properties that one tries to describe, thus posing an inductive bias.

The hidden fermion formalism describes the MM physical degrees of freedom as the projection of an augmented Hilbert space with Mtot=M+M~M_{\text{tot}}=M+\tilde{M} degrees of freedom. The augmented Hilbert space is partitioned into MM visible and M~\tilde{M} hidden degrees of freedom. The MM visible modes are a copy of the physical degrees of freedom. The projection is applied as follows: the occupancy of the visible modes 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} matches the occupancy of the physical degrees of freedom, while the occupancy of the hidden modes 𝐱~\tilde{{\mathbf{x}}} by the N~\tilde{N} hidden fermions is unequivocally determined by the occupancy of the visible modes. This correspondence can be summarized by a constraint function: 𝐱~=F⁡(𝐱)\tilde{{\mathbf{x}}}=F({\mathbf{x}}), which must be permutation-invariant. The numbers of hidden modes and particles are hyper-parameters to be chosen by the user. The variational wave-function amplitudes are obtained as the overlap between a basis state and a parametrized Slater determinant in the augmented Hilbert space |ΨSD⟩\ket{\Psi_\text{SD}}, characterized by N+N~N+\tilde{N} orbital functions, projected into the physical subspace:

ψθ​(𝐱)=⟨𝐱,F⁡(𝐱)|​|ΨSD⟩.\psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})=\bra{\xx, F(\xx)}\ket{\Psi_\text{SD}}. (55)

An extremely flexible wave function ansatz is obtained when the constraint function is parametrized F→FθF\rightarrow F_{\theta} and when M~→∞\tilde{M}\rightarrow\infty, even if MM is countable [26]. This ansatz can represent Slater-Jastrow states, as well as backflow wave functions. Furthermore, it can be explicitly spanned as the linear combination of all possible single, double, …, N~\tilde{N}-tuple particle excitations from the Hartree-Fock ground state to the N~\tilde{N} lowest unoccupied orbitals in the Hartree-Fock basis. Furthermore, the wave function amplitude evaluation in this formalism is straightforward, as shown in Fig. 5.

This family of variational states has demonstrated high degrees of accuracy in the description of the ground state properties of the Hubbard model in square and cylinder-like geometries [26], as well as in the fully-connected lattice [11]. Furthermore, this variational ansatz class has received increasing interest for the description of interacting nucleons [102, 104, 103].

III.2.5 Single-particle basis considerations

The accuracy in the description of fermionic wave-functions by classical approximations is strongly affected by the single-particle basis choice that is used to span the Hilbert space, within a basis set [111, 114, 119]. The single-particle basis can be transformed according to:

|ϕ~α⟩=∑pΞp​α​|ϕp⟩,\ket*{\widetilde{\phi} _\alpha}=\sum_{p}\Xi_{p\alpha}\ket{\phi_p}, (56)

where Ξ∈ℂNorb×Norb\Xi\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\text{orb}}\times N_{\text{orb}}} is the unitary matrix describing the change of basis. This class of changes of bases are know as single-particle basis transformations. The functional form of the Hamiltonian in Eq. 42 remains the same, but the coefficients are transformed according to the tensor transformations:

hp​q→∑p​qhp​q​Ξp​α​Ξq​β;hp​q​r​s→∑p​q​r​shp​q​r​s​Ξp​α​Ξq​β​Ξr​δ​Ξs​γ.\begin{gathered}h_{pq}\rightarrow\sum_{pq}h_{pq}\Xi_{p\alpha}\Xi_{q\beta};\\ h_{pqrs}\rightarrow\sum_{pqrs}h_{pqrs}\Xi_{p\alpha}\Xi_{q\beta}\Xi_{r\delta}\Xi_{s\gamma}.\end{gathered} (57)

For example, when considering molecular systems in the Hartree-Fock (molecular orbital) basis, the ground state wave function amplitudes are dominated by the electronic configuration corresponding to the occupation of the NN Hartree-Fock orbitals of lowest energy, while the amplitudes for other configurations rapidly decay. This sparse structure can be hard to capture by non-determinant based states [114, 119]. The Markov-Chain sampling of sparse (in the space of electronic configurations) wave functions can require a large number of samples to converge. Furthermore, wave functions dominated by zero-amplitude components pose challenges when estimating gμg_{\mu} and Sμ​νS_{\mu\nu} in Eq. 16 [14].

More generally, the issue lies on the lack of invariance under the reparametrization of the Hamiltonian given by single-particle basis transformations. To address this issue, the variational state |ψθ⟩\ket{\psi_\theta} can be dressed by a parametrized Gaussian unitary operator [119]

U⁡(κ)=exp⁡(∑p​qκp​q​ap†​aq),U(\kappa)=\exp\left(\sum_{pq}\kappa_{pq}a^{\dagger}_{p}a_{q}\right)\;, (58)

yielding the variational state |ψ{κ,θ}⟩=U⁡(κ)​|ψθ⟩\ket*{\psi_{\{\kappa, \theta\}}}=U(\kappa)\ket{\psi_\theta}. Both κ\kappa and θ\theta variational parameters are treated on equal footing. Since the action of U⁡(κ)U(\kappa) on a basis state |𝐱⟩\ket{\xx} yields an anti-symmetric product state on a rotated single-particle basis [158], then the state |ψ{κ,θ}⟩\ket*{\psi_{\{\kappa, \theta\}}} is invariant under single-particle basis transformations. It has been empirically demonstrated that the expressive power and optimization landscape are improved when a NQS is dressed by U⁡(κ)U(\kappa) in a collection of molecular systems and the Hubbard model [119].

III.3 Unitary operations

III.3.1 Real-time evolution

In recent years, an increasing body of research has been dedicated to real-time evolution of neural-network quantum states. As described in Sec. II.5, time-stepping is performed by projecting the state transformed by the unitary propagator onto the variational manifold: ψθ+δ​θ​(𝐱)=⟨𝐱|​e−i​H​δ​t​|ψθ⟩\psi_{\theta+\delta\theta}({\mathbf{x}})=\bra{\xx}e^{-iH\delta t}\ket{\psi_\theta}, for a general trial state ψθ\psi_{\theta}. The precise way this projection is performed has been a focus point of the community.

Authors in Refs. [66, 67] focus on bosonic models on the lattice. As a concrete example, consider the prototypical Bose-Hubbard model

H=−t∑⟨p,q⟩(bp†bq+bq†bp)+U2∑pnp(np−1),H=-t\sum_{\langle p,q\rangle}\left(b^{\dagger}_{p}b_{q}+b^{\dagger}_{q}b_{p}\right)+\frac{U}{2}\sum_{p}n_{p}(n_{p}-1)\;, (59)

where bib_{i} and bi†b^{\dagger}_{i} are bosonic annihilation and creation operators, respectfully, and ni=bi†​bin_{i}=b_{i}^{\dagger}b_{i} is the number operator used to label computational basis states {|n1,…,nN⟩:ni∈ℕ0}\left\{\ket{n_1, \ldots, n_N}\;:n_{i}\in\mathbbm{N}_{0}\right\}. The Hamiltonian in Eq. 59 should be thought of as a direct bosonic counterpart of Eq. 43.

For such a system of lattice bosons and an initial state |ψ⁡(t=0)⟩=|ψ0⟩\ket{\psi(t=0)}=\ket{\psi_0}, a simple Jastrow-type [127] wavefunction can be constructed as:

|ψ⁡(t)⟩=exp⁡(∑μθμ​(t)​𝒜μ​(n))​|ψ0⟩\ket{\psi(t)}=\exp\left(\sum_{\mu}\theta_{\mu}(t)\;\mathcal{A}_{\mu}(n)\right)\ket{\psi_0} (60)

where operators 𝒜μ\mathcal{A}_{\mu} are usually chosen on physical grounds as important excitations of the initial state. Authors in Ref. [66] choose two-site correlations 𝒜μ→𝒜k​(n)=∑ini​ni+k\mathcal{A}_{\mu}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}_{k}(n)=\sum_{i}n_{i}n_{i+k}, successfully reproducing glassy quench dynamics of long-lived metastable states. Authors in Ref. [159, 160] use a variational state of the form outlined in Eq. 60 but guide their choices of 𝒜μ\mathcal{A}_{\mu} by the cumulant expansion of the underlying classical Hamiltonian. The same type of state has been used to suggest local gauge invariance as a mechanism for disorder-free localization [161] in two dimensional spin models.

As described in Sec. II.4, in practice the logarithm ln⁡ψθ⁡(t)​(𝐱)=ln⁡⟨𝐱|ψ⁡(t)⟩\ln\psi_{\theta(t)}({\mathbf{x}})=\ln\innerproduct{\xx}{\psi(t) } is directly parametrized instead of the wavefunction itself. In mathematical language, it is then trivial to show that the trial state in Eq. 60 corresponds to a linear model with physically-motivated pairwise kernel functions [162, 2] 𝒜μ→𝒜⁡(ni,nj)\mathcal{A}_{\mu}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}(n_{i},n_{j}).

As an example of a more complex trial state for Fermi-Hubbard dynamics 43, authors in Ref. [68] consider a symmetry-projected Gutzwiller-Slater-Jastrow-Backflow wavefunction. This scheme introduces parametrized kernels into a Jastrow-type state outlined in Eq. 60, reproducing real-time dependence of a range of physically relevant observables.

In contrast with hand-crafted and fine-tuned trial states designed to capture known dynamical processes, the advent of automatic differentiation and large-scale adoption of NQS opened the door to expressive black-box wavefunctions. Apart from improvements to ground-state results discussed, these trial states can capture accurate time-evolution over a range of physical Hamiltonians.

Authors in Ref. [30, 163] employ a deep feed-forward convolutional neural network (CNN) to explore the transverse-field Ising model

H=−J∑⟨i,j⟩σziσzj−h∑iσxi,H=-J\sum_{\left\langle i,j\right\rangle}\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}-h\sum_{i}\sigma^{x}_{i}\;, (61)

whose dynamics has recently been shown to be accessible in Rydberg atom experiments [164, 165, 166] and superconducting quantum devices [167]. We note that the Hamiltonian in Eq. 61 is a special case of Eq. 37.

In Ref. [30], large square lattice dynamics, up to 12×1212\times 12, have been treated using direct integration of the t-VMC Eq. 16. When using deeper models like CNNs, in contrast with Eq. 60, regularizing the inverse of the SS matrix (Eq. 16) becomes crucial. Ref. [30] employs a custom spectral inverse, allowing the underlying calculations to proceed to ∼10​J−1\sim 10\,J^{-1} using very thorough Monte Carlo sampling at each step. Collapse and revival oscillations of ferromagnetic order are observed. Universal near-critical dynamics have been explored in Ref. [163] within the context of quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism [168, 169] in two dimensions. More recently, experimentally observable spectral functions have also been extracted from related t-VMC calculations [170]. Disordered long-time dynamics of the Hamiltonian in Eq. 61 have been studied in Ref. [171], including local unitary transformations in the NQS in a way similar to Sec. II.6.

Generally, noise in estimators of matrix elements in Eq. 16 can conspire to render the SS matrix singular by making small eigenvalues vanish. Therefore, quickly and efficiently obtaining many uncorrelated samples from |ψ|2\left|\psi\right|^{2} is crucial. In addition, neural-network wavefunctions are usually overparametrized by design. While considered beneficial in AI applications [172], this feature can produce linearly dependent or vanishing rows and columns in SS. Therefore, choosing an efficiently parameterized state is equally important. This leads to a superficially counter-intuitive observation – adding more parameters to a trial state can reduce accuracy by making SS ill-conditioned.

Authors in Ref. [31] perform a large simulation of the quantum rotor model

H=−g​J2∑k∂2∂ϕk2−J∑⟨k,l⟩cos⁡(ϕk−ϕl),H=-\frac{gJ}{2}\sum_{k}\partialderivative[2]{\phi_k}-J\sum_{\langle k,l\rangle}\cos(\phi_k - \phi_l)\;, (62)

describing a system of continuous planar rotors on a lattice. An advantage of the NQS treatment is that one can work directly in a continuous basis |ϕ⟩=|ϕ1,…,ϕN⟩\ket{\bm{\phi}}=\ket{\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_N} of individual rotor angles ϕi\phi_{i}, bypassing discretization or local basis truncation that bias similar tensor-network approaches. The expression in Eq. 62 is an effective Hamiltonian that captures the physics of superconducting Josephson junctions [173, 174, 175, 176, 177] that can be used to model phenomena related to superconducting or transmon qubit systems [178].

Using a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler introduced in Sec. II.3, calculations in Ref. [31] reduce the sampling overhead encountered in previous works while maintaining good accuracy. In addition, the SS matrix inverse is regularized by a simple adaptive spectral regularization introduced in Eq. 25 with the weight function

w⁡(σ2)=[1+(λ2/σ2)6]−1w(\sigma^{2})=\left[1+\left(\nicefrac{{\lambda^{2}}}{{\sigma^{2}}}\right)^{6}\right]^{-1} (63)

where λ2\lambda^{2} is set automatically at each step as a function of the spectrum {σ12,…,σP2}\left\{\sigma^{2}_{1},\ldots,\sigma^{2}_{P}\right\}. This setup mitigates the underlying numerical instability for the CNN trial wavefunction, allowing accurate simulations up to ∼10​J−1\sim 10\,J^{-1} for 8×88\times 8 lattices and access to nontrivial observables such as the Loschmidt echo and the vorticity.

Due to the inversion problem described above, several alternatives to direct integration of the top-level differential equation θ˙=−S−1​f\dot{\theta}=-S^{-1}f have been proposed. Authors in Refs. [32, 14, 33] choose to completely replace the troublesome pseudoinverse with optimization subproblems at each step in real time. Specifically, Ref. [14] formulates this projection step as a minimization of the quantum infidelity (see Sec. II.6)

θ⁡(t+δ​t)=argminθ′𝒟​(|ψθ′⟩,e−i​H​δ​t​|ψθ⁡(t)⟩)\theta(t+\delta t)=\argmin_{\theta^{\prime}}\mathcal{D}\left(\ket{\psi_{\theta'}},e^{-iH\delta t}\ket*{\psi_{\theta(t)}}\right) (64)

between the exact propagation of the state at time tt and its projection onto the variational manifold. Apart from avoiding numerical problems, authors report that this framework removes the bias appearing in estimators in Eq. 16 and Eq. 24 when ψ⁡(𝐱)≈0\psi({\mathbf{x}})\approx 0 (see Sec. II.4). The key observation is that the gradients of the infidelity objective in Eq. 64 can be efficiently optimized using canned optimizers like Adam [62] if one exploits the Trotter approximation

e−i​H​δ​t=e−i⁡(H0+HI)​δ​t≈e−i​H0​δ​t2​e−i​HI​δ​t​e−i​H0​δ​t2e^{-iH\delta t}=e^{-i(H_{0}+H_{I})\delta t}\approx e^{-iH_{0}\frac{\delta t}{2}}e^{-iH_{I}\delta t}e^{-iH_{0}\frac{\delta t}{2}} (65)

in Eq. 64, assuming that the system Hamiltonian H=H0+HIH=H_{0}+H_{I} decomposes into a term local in the computational basis H0H_{0} and an interaction term HIH_{I}. Eliminating numerical instabilities, determining the scaling and reducing the computational cost of similar projective methods is an area of open research.

III.3.2 Quantum circuit simulation

Quantum circuits offer a different perspective on unitary operations to NQS. In principle, arbitrarily complex unitary operators can be applied to |ψθ⟩\ket{\psi_\theta} if one has a way of implementing a set of universal quantum logical gates [179].

Authors in Ref. [180] choose the following one-qubit gates: RZ​(ϕ)=diag​(1,ei​ϕ)\textrm{RZ}(\phi)={\text{diag}}(1,e^{i\phi}),

H=12​(111−1)\textrm{H}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\endlx@physics@matrix) (66)

and the two-qubit gate CZ​(ϕ)=diag​(1,1,1,ei​ϕ)\textrm{CZ}(\phi)={\text{diag}}(1,1,1,e^{i\phi}). In that case, an analytical property of RBMs can be exploited – both diagonal gates can be applied exactly (with fidelity 11) by direct substitution rules in parameter space.

However, implementing the remaining Hadamard gate H is nontrivial. The key observation is that any unitary 𝒰\mathcal{U} can be approximated by minimizing the infidelity 𝒟⁡(ψθ′,𝒰​ψθ)\mathcal{D}(\psi_{\theta^{\prime}},\mathcal{U}\psi_{\theta}) with respect to θ′\theta^{\prime}. Setting 𝒰→H\mathcal{U}\rightarrow\textrm{H}, one obtains a recipe for approximating the state H​|ψθ⟩\textrm{H}\ket{\psi_\theta} for any θ\theta. Calculations in Refs. [180, 34] show that this scheme can be used to obtain excellent approximations of Hadamard and Fourier transforms of entangled initial states.

Authors in Ref. [34] show that upgrading the optimizer to SR within the framework of Eq. 29 allows one to simulate deep quantum circuits. They focus on the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) [181, 182], whose structure is outlined on Fig. 6. Taking advantage of exact gate application, the simple computation in Ref. [34] successfully reaches 54 qubits at p=4p=4 QAOA layers, approximately implementing 324 ZZ-rotation gates and 216 X-rotation gates without large-scale computational resources.

III.4 Quantum state tomography and reconstruction

In contrast to the circuit simulation case in which the target state is known at each step, reconstructing a neural-network quantum state with only measurement data has been an open problem since the seminal work in Ref. [35]. Exploiting the mathematical machinery of Sec. II.7, authors in Refs. [35, 70, 69] directly minimize the many-basis KL-divergence cost in Eq. 31. Restricted Boltzmann machines were (Eq.38) were used to capture both pure state and density matrix representations of reconstructed states.

Data-driven enhancements of VMC approach of the Rydberg Hamiltonian have been considered as well in Ref. [86, 183], showing that any amount of experimental measurement data can be used to efficiently pretrain an RNN model, drastically reducing computation time.

Finally, authors in Ref. [184] show that NQS based on the transformer [185] architecture can be trained on data generated by a variational quantum algorithm to enhance accuracy and decrease error bars.

IV Concluding remarks and outlook

Neural network parametrization of quantum states is a promising avenue to study systems of interacting quantum particles. The outstanding expressive power of this family if variational wave functions has allowed to obtain results which are competitive with other state-of-the-art quantum many-body methods in challenging many-body systems.

There are a number challenges that this variational family faces, most of which are related to the optimization of the large number of variational parameters they posses. The first challenge is the calculation and inversion of the SS matrix for large models, which may become expensive to realize and numerically unstable to invert. A solution has been proposed to greatly reduce the cost of evaluating and inverting SS [22]. NQS rely on gradients to optimize the wave function parameters. Another difficulty arises when the support of the wave function does not coincide with the support of the gradients. In this case, the Monte Carlo estimator for the gradients and the components of SS contains a bias [14]. While the bias for gradients can be removed, the bias for SS remains an open problem [14]. A solution based on overlap optimization is proposed in [14, 186]. Generally, there is lack in the understanding of the characteristics of the optimization landscape of NQS parametrizations. Initial progress has been made in its characterization using neural tangent kernel techniques in the limit of infinite width NQS [187]. However, there are still open questions in practical implementations with finite numbers of parameters.

Another challenge that these architectures face is the study of realistic systems of interacting electrons in second quantization. The number of terms in the Hamiltonian in Eq. 42 grows with the fourth power of the number of orbitals. The cost of evaluating the local energy for a moderate number of samples becomes prohibitively expensive, thus limiting the sizes of the basis sets that can be used for the simulation of realistic fermionic systems. Thus far, this has prevented any kind of extrapolation to the complete basis-set limit, which is possible in other many-body methods. A possible solution is to use the inductive bias where a the wave function amplitudes for a large number of electronic configurations is set to zero (active space calculation). In this case the choice of the single particle basis strongly affects the success of the highly compact wave function representation. Ref. [119] demonstrates the first active space NQS calculation with orbital optimizations, thus paving the path towards the study of more realistic fermionic systems using active spaces beyond the scope of exact diagonalization. While MPS in conjunction with DMRG can be used to represent the wave function in the active space [188, 189, 190, 191, 192], this wave function representation is limited by the amount of entanglement entropy that it can sustain.

Efficient real-time calculations also remain a challenge. With significant advances in neural-network architectures [2, 30] and Monte-Carlo sampling [31], larger systems can be simulated for a longer time, reaching experimentally relevant system sizes and time scales in some cases. However, scaling the t-VMC approach to even larger systems and NQS will likely require rethinking the method itself – the QGT matrix SS inverse is a clear bottleneck. Alternative approaches have been proposed [14, 193, 194] and scaling them up is an area of active research.

Neural network quantum states remain a powerful way of compressing complex many-body quantum physics. As model architectures, optimization algorithms and researchers’ intuition evolve, these methods are entering the domain of practical application, especially in quantum chemistry and benchmarking near-term quantum hardware.

Appendix A Derivation of the projected equations of motion

In Eq. 15 in the main text, a simple update scheme for variational parameters is presented:

|Ψθ+δ​θ⟩=e−δ​τ​H​|Ψθ⟩\ket{\Psi_{\theta+ \delta\theta}}=e^{-\delta\tau H}\ket{\Psi_\theta} (67)

where |Ψθ⟩=|ψ⟩/⟨ψ|ψ⟩\ket{\Psi_\theta}=\ket{\psi}/\sqrt{\innerproduct{\psi}{\psi}} is the normalized version of our variational state of choice, turning the proportionality sign in Eq. 15 into an equality. We note that the differential version of Eq. 67, ddτ​|Ψθ⟩=−H​|Ψθ⟩\frac{\differential}{\differential\tau}\ket{\Psi_\theta}=-H\ket{\Psi_\theta} is known as the Bloch equation and can serve as an equivalent starting point for the following analysis.

In this appendix, we derive the projected equations of motion given in Eq. 16 for variational parameters θ\theta. We note that the following derivation plays out almost identically for the case of real-time evolution, upon substitution δ​τ→i​δ​t\delta\tau\rightarrow i\delta t. Borrowing notational conventions set up in Sec. II, we begin by Taylor-expanding both sides of Eq. 15 in small parameters:

e−δ​τ​H​|Ψθ⟩=(𝟙−δ​τ​H)​|Ψθ⟩+⋯|Ψθ+δ​θ⟩=|Ψθ⟩+∑μδ​θμ​∂μ|Ψθ⟩=(𝟙+∑μδ​θμ​𝒟μ)​|Ψθ⟩+⋯.\begin{gathered}e^{-\delta\tau H}\ket{\Psi_{\theta}}=\left(\mathbbm{1}-\delta\tau H\right)\ket{\Psi_{\theta}}+\cdots\\ \ket{\Psi_{\theta+ \delta\theta}}=\ket{\Psi_{\theta}}+\sum_{\mu}\delta\theta^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\ket{\Psi_{\theta}}=\left(\mathbbm{1}+\sum_{\mu}\delta\theta^{\mu}\mathcal{D}_{\mu}\right)\ket{\Psi_{\theta}}+\cdots\,.\end{gathered} (68)

where we exploit the following chain of identities

∂μ|Ψθ⟩=∑𝐱∂μΨθ​(𝐱)​|𝐱⟩=∑𝐱Ψθ​(𝐱)​∂μln⁡Ψθ​(𝐱)​|𝐱⟩=(∑𝐱′∂μln⁡Ψθ​(𝐱)​|𝐱′⟩⟨𝐱′|)​(∑𝐱Ψθ​(𝐱)​|𝐱⟩)=𝒟μ​|ψθ⟩\partial_{\mu}\ket{\Psi_{\theta}}=\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\partial_{\mu}\Psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})\ket{\xx}=\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\Psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})\,\partial_{\mu}\ln\Psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})\ket{\xx}=\left(\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}}\partial_{\mu}\ln\Psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})\outerproduct{\xx'}{\xx'}\right)\left(\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\Psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})\ket{\xx}\right)=\mathcal{D}_{\mu}\ket{\psi_\theta} (69)

to construct a convenient representation of derivative operators

∂μ↦𝒟μ=∑𝐱∂μlnΨθ(𝐱)|𝐱⟩⟨𝐱|\partial_{\mu}\mapsto\mathcal{D}_{\mu}=\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}}\partial_{\mu}\ln\Psi_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})\outerproduct{\xx}{\xx} (70)

on the variational manifold ℳψ\mathcal{M}_{\psi}. Truncating the Taylor expansions in Eq. 68, we get

∑μ𝒟μ​|Ψθ⟩​θ˙μ=−H​|Ψθ⟩\sum_{\mu}\mathcal{D}_{\mu}\ket{\Psi_\theta}\dot{\theta}^{\mu}=-H\ket{\Psi_\theta} (71)

and reduce the original equation to finding θ˙μ=argmin‖∑μ𝒟μ​θ˙μ−H‖\dot{\theta}^{\mu}=\argmin\norm{\sum_\mu\mathcal{D} _\mu\dot{\theta} ^\mu- H}. To build a convenient way of solving for θ˙\dot{\theta}, we left-multiply by ⟨Ψθ|​𝒟ν†\bra{\Psi_\theta}\mathcal{D}^{\dagger}_{\nu} and relabel indices:

∑ν⟨𝒟μ†​𝒟ν⟩Ψθ​θ˙ν=−⟨𝒟μ†​H⟩Ψθ,\sum_{\nu}\expectationvalue{ \mathcal{D} _\mu^\dagger\mathcal{D} _\nu}_{\Psi_{\theta}}\dot{\theta}^{\nu}=-\expectationvalue{ \mathcal{D} _\mu^\dagger H}_{\Psi_{\theta}}\;, (72)

yielding a linear system.

Finally, we need to unpack the fact that we usually do not have access to the full normalized state |Ψ⟩\ket{\Psi}. Instead, we need to substitute |Ψ⟩↦|ψ⟩/⟨ψ|ψ⟩\ket{\Psi}\mapsto\ket{\psi}/\sqrt{\innerproduct{\psi}{\psi}}. The expectation value changes trivially into the form that can be evaluated using Monte Carlo sampling, as discussed in the main text. However, variational derivative operators 𝒟μ\mathcal{D}_{\mu} pick up an extra term because

∂μln⁡Ψ=∂μln⁡ψθ−12​⟨∂μψθ|ψθ⟩+⟨ψθ|∂μψθ⟩⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩=∂μln⁡ψθ−Re⟨𝒪μ⟩ψθ\partial_{\mu}\ln\Psi=\partial_{\mu}\ln\psi_{\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\innerproduct{\partial_\mu\psi_\theta}{\psi_\theta}+\innerproduct{\psi_\theta}{\partial_\mu\psi_\theta}}{\innerproduct{\psi_\theta}{\psi_\theta}}=\partial_{\mu}\ln\psi_{\theta}-\real\expectationvalue{\OO_\mu}_{\psi_{\theta}} (73)

assuming that |∂μψθ⟩=∂μ|ψθ⟩\ket{\partial_\mu\psi_\theta}=\partial_{\mu}\ket{\psi_\theta} and that all of the variational parameters θ\theta are real: θ∈ℝP\theta\in\mathbbm{R}^{P}. Therefore, we are free to substitute 𝒟μ↦𝒪μ−Re⟨𝒪μ⟩\mathcal{D}_{\mu}\mapsto\mathcal{O}_{\mu}-\real\expectationvalue{\OO_\mu} in Eq. 72, resulting in

Re∑ν{⟨𝒪μ†​𝒪ν⟩ψθ−⟨𝒪μ†⟩ψθ⟨𝒪ν⟩ψθ}θ˙ν=−Re{⟨𝒪μ†​H⟩Ψθ−⟨𝒪μ†⟩ψθ⟨H⟩ψθ},\real\sum_{\nu}\left\{\expectationvalue{ \OO_\mu^\dagger\OO_\nu}_{\psi_{\theta}}-\expectationvalue{ \OO_\mu^\dagger}_{\psi_{\theta}}\expectationvalue{\OO_\nu}_{\psi_{\theta}}\right\}\dot{\theta}^{\nu}=-\real\left\{\expectationvalue{ \OO_\mu^\dagger H}_{\Psi_{\theta}}-\expectationvalue{ \OO_\mu^\dagger}_{\psi_{\theta}}\expectationvalue{H}_{\psi_{\theta}}\right\}\;, (74)

which is identical to expressions in Eq. 16 in the main text.
